cos(2π − x) = cos x, sin(2π − x) = −sin x.

example.q: Find cos 15° using cos(x − y).

learn.reallife: Phase-shift tricks such as cos(π/2 − x) = sin x are used in electrical engineering to compare AC voltages that are out of step.

games.title: Derive cos(x − y) from cos(x + y)
items: Start with cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y.
Use cos(−y) = cos y and sin(−y) = −sin y.
cos(x − y) = cos x cos y + sin x sin y.

quiz.q: cos(x + y) equals:
options: cos x cos y + sin x sin y
sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos x cos y − sin x sin y
quiz.explain: The sign between the terms is opposite to the sign inside: '+' inside gives '−' outside for cosine.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cos(x − y) sign

quiz.q: cos(π − x) equals:
quiz.explain: π − x is in quadrant II for acute x, where cos is negative. π is an even multiple of π/2, so the function stays cos: cos(π − x) = −cos x.
quiz.mistake: Switches cos to sin for a π shift

quiz.q: Find the value of cos 70° cos 10° + sin 70° sin 10°.
quiz.explain: This is cos(70° − 10°) = cos 60° = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos(70° + 10°) = cos 80°

quiz.q: sin(π/2 + x) equals:
quiz.explain: For acute x, π/2 + x is in quadrant II where sin is positive; π/2 changes sin to cos.
quiz.mistake: Gives the sign of cos in quadrant II

quiz.q: What is cos 105°?
quiz.explain: cos(60° + 45°) = cos 60° cos 45° − sin 60° sin 45° = (1 − √3)/(2√2) = (√2 − √6)/4, a negative number as expected in quadrant II.
quiz.mistake: Uses the plus sign of cos(x − y)

quiz.q: Simplify sin(π/3 + x) cos x − cos(π/3 + x) sin x.
quiz.explain: This is sin[(π/3 + x) − x] = sin(π/3) = √3/2; the x cancels completely.
quiz.mistake: Adds the angles instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Find cos 330°.
quiz.explain: cos(360° − 30°) = cos 30° = √3/2; cos is positive in quadrant IV.
quiz.mistake: Thinks every value in quadrant IV is negative

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): cos(−x) = cos x for every x.
Reason (R): Putting x = 0 in cos(x − y) gives cos(−y) = cos 0 cos y + sin 0 sin y = cos y.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and R actually derives A from the cos(x − y) formula.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R is a proof of A

teach.ask: Gappu is lost in allied angles like cos(π − x) and sin(π/2 + x). Explain the cos(x + y) formula and a quick rule for allied angles.
teach.praise: π shifts keep the function, π/2 shifts swap it, and the quadrant gives the sign. I'm a pro now!
teach.nudge: When does sin turn into cos — with a π shift or a π/2 shift?

topics.title: sin(x ± y), tan(x ± y) and exact values

learn.hook: Your calculator knows sin 15°, but can you get its exact surd value with just 45° and 30°? Sum and difference formulas say yes.
points: sin(x + y) = sin x cos y + cos x sin y; sin(x − y) = sin x cos y − cos x sin y.
tan(x + y) = (tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y), tan(x − y) = (tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y), when the tangents and the result are defined.
cot(x + y) = (cot x cot y − 1)/(cot y + cot x); cot(x − y) = (cot x cot y + 1)/(cot y − cot x).
To prove an identity, expand the compound angles, use allied-angle values, and simplify one side to the other.

example.q: Find tan(π/4 + x) in terms of tan x.
steps: tan(π/4 + x) = (tan π/4 + tan x)/(1 − tan π/4 · tan x).

learn.reallife: Surveyors computing the height of a hill in the Western Ghats from two angles of elevation often combine angles with tan(x − y).

games.title: Match the expansion
pairs: sin x cos y + cos x sin y
sin x cos y − cos x sin y
(tan x + tan y)/(1 − tan x tan y)
(tan x − tan y)/(1 + tan x tan y)
(cot x cot y − 1)/(cot y + cot x)

quiz.q: sin(x − y) equals:
options: sin x cos y + cos x sin y
cos x cos y − sin x sin y
sin x cos y − cos x sin y
sin x sin y − cos x cos y
quiz.explain: For sine, the sign between the terms matches the sign inside the bracket.
quiz.mistake: Uses the cosine sign rule for sine

quiz.q: Find sin 40° cos 20° + cos 40° sin 20°.
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(40° − 20°)

quiz.q: If tan A = 1/2 and tan B = 1/3, then tan(A + B) is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator 1 − tan A tan B

quiz.q: tan(13π/12) equals:
quiz.explain: 13π/12 = π + π/12 and tan has period π, so tan(13π/12) = tan(π/12) = tan 15° = 2 − √3.
quiz.mistake: Treats π + x like π − x and flips the sign

quiz.q: If tan x = 3 and tan y = 2, find tan(x − y).
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 − tan x tan y in the denominator

quiz.q: The value of sin 75° is:
quiz.mistake: Mixes up sin 75° with sin 15°

quiz.q: Simplify cos 4x cos x + sin 4x sin x.
quiz.explain: This is cos(4x − x) = cos 3x, using cos(A − B) = cos A cos B + sin A sin B.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos(A + B) and gets cos 5x

quiz.q: If sin A = 3/5 and cos B = 5/13, with A and B acute, find sin(A + B).
quiz.mistake: Uses sin(A − B) or cos(A + B)

teach.ask: Gappu wants sin 75° exactly, without a calculator. Explain the sin(x + y) and tan(x + y) formulas and use them.
teach.praise: 75° = 45° + 30°, and the formula does the rest. Exact and elegant!
teach.nudge: Which two familiar angles add up to 75°?

learn.hook: Put y = x in the sum formulas and you get the double-angle formulas — the most-used identities in Class 11 and 12 calculus.
points: sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x = 2 tan x/(1 + tan²x).
cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x = 2cos²x − 1 = 1 − 2sin²x = (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x).
tan 2x = 2 tan x/(1 − tan²x).
sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x; cos 3x = 4 cos³x − 3 cos x; tan 3x = (3 tan x − tan³x)/(1 − 3 tan²x).
Half angles: cos x = 2cos²(x/2) − 1 = 1 − 2sin²(x/2). Take the square root, then choose the sign from the quadrant of x/2.

example.q: If tan x = −3/4 and x lies in quadrant II, find sin(x/2), cos(x/2) and tan(x/2).
steps: x in quadrant II ⇒ π/2 < x < π ⇒ π/4 < x/2 < π/2, so all half-angle values are positive.

learn.reallife: The formula sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x tells a cricket coach that a ball thrown at 45° goes farthest (ignoring air resistance), because sin 90° = 1 is the largest.

games.title: Derive cos 2x = 2cos²x − 1
items: cos(x + y) = cos x cos y − sin x sin y
Put y = x: cos 2x = cos²x − sin²x

quiz.q: If sin x = 3/5 and x is acute, then sin 2x is:
quiz.mistake: Doubles sin x instead of using 2 sin x cos x

quiz.q: If cos x = 1/3, then cos 2x is:
quiz.mistake: Doubles cos x

quiz.q: If tan x = 1/2, then tan 2x is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the denominator 1 − tan²x

quiz.q: cos 3x equals:
quiz.explain: cos 3x = 4cos³x − 3cos x; note the order is reversed compared with sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x.
quiz.mistake: Copies the pattern of sin 3x

quiz.q: Using sin 3x = 3 sin x − 4 sin³x, find sin 3x when sin x = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Cubes 1/2 as 1/6

quiz.q: If cos x = −1/3 and x lies in quadrant III, find sin(x/2).
quiz.mistake: Takes the sign from the quadrant of x instead of x/2

quiz.q: Which expression equals (1 − tan²x)/(1 + tan²x)?
quiz.explain: Divide cos²x − sin²x by cos²x + sin²x = 1, then divide top and bottom by cos²x.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with the tan 2x formula

quiz.q: Simplify 2 sin 15° cos 15°.
quiz.explain: 2 sin x cos x = sin 2x, so the value is sin 30° = 1/2.
quiz.mistake: Doubles the angle twice to get sin 60°

teach.ask: Gappu forgot all three forms of cos 2x before the test. Explain how to get them from cos(x + y), and how to pick the sign for half angles.
teach.praise: One formula, three faces — and the half angle decides its own sign. Super!
teach.nudge: For sin(x/2), whose quadrant decides the sign: x or x/2?

learn.hook: When two tabla notes of nearly equal pitch play together, you hear 'beats'. The maths behind it is sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x+y)/2) cos((x−y)/2).
points: cos x + cos y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); cos x − cos y = −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
sin x + sin y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) cos((x − y)/2); sin x − sin y = 2 cos((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y); −2 sin x sin y = cos(x + y) − cos(x − y).
2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y); 2 cos x sin y = sin(x + y) − sin(x − y).
Proving identities: convert sums to products (or products to sums), cancel common factors, then use allied or double-angle results.

example.q: Prove that (cos 9x + cos 3x)/(sin 9x − sin 3x) = cot 3x.

learn.reallife: Radio engineers mix two signals by multiplying them; the product-to-sum formula 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) shows the new frequencies that appear.

games.title: Spot the correct formula
items: 2 sin x cos y = sin(x + y) + sin(x − y)
Add the expansions of sin(x + y) and sin(x − y).
cos x − cos y = 2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2)
There is a minus sign in front: −2 sin((x + y)/2) sin((x − y)/2).
2 sin x sin y = cos(x − y) − cos(x + y)
This is −2 sin x sin y = cos(x + y) − cos(x − y) rearranged.

quiz.q: sin 5x + sin 3x equals:
quiz.explain: sin A + sin B = 2 sin((A + B)/2) cos((A − B)/2) = 2 sin 4x cos x.
quiz.mistake: Uses the pattern for sin A − sin B

quiz.q: cos 6x − cos 2x equals:
quiz.explain: cos A − cos B = −2 sin((A + B)/2) sin((A − B)/2) with A = 6x, B = 2x.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: Find the exact value of cos 75° + cos 15°.
quiz.mistake: Adds cos 75° and cos 15° as cos 90°

quiz.q: 2 cos 45° cos 15° equals:
quiz.explain: 2 cos x cos y = cos(x + y) + cos(x − y) = cos 60° + cos 30°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up with the sin product formula

quiz.q: Find the value of sin 105° + cos 105°.
quiz.mistake: Thinks sin 105° and cos 105° cancel

quiz.q: Simplify (sin 5x − sin 3x)/(cos 5x + cos 3x).
quiz.explain: Numerator 2 cos 4x sin x, denominator 2 cos 4x cos x; the ratio is tan x.
quiz.mistake: Cancels the wrong factor and keeps 4x

quiz.q: 2 sin 3x cos x equals:
quiz.explain: 2 sin A cos B = sin(A + B) + sin(A − B) = sin 4x + sin 2x.
quiz.mistake: Adds the angles without forming the sum and difference

quiz.q: Find the exact value of sin 75° − sin 15°.
quiz.mistake: Uses cos 30° instead of sin 30°

teach.ask: Gappu needs to simplify (cos 9x + cos 3x)/(sin 9x − sin 3x). Explain the sum-to-product formulas and the half-sum, half-difference idea.
teach.praise: Half-sum and half-difference — sums turn into products and things cancel. Woohoo!
teach.nudge: When you add two cosines, which two new angles appear in the product?

topics.title: The imaginary unit i and complex numbers

learn.hook: No real number squared gives −1. So mathematicians invented one: i. Today electrical engineers at power grids use it every day.
points: x² + 1 = 0 has no real solution, because x² ≥ 0 for every real x. We extend R by a new number i with i² = −1.
A complex number is z = a + ib with a, b real. Re z = a is the real part and Im z = b is the imaginary part. The set of complex numbers is C.
If b = 0, z = a is purely real; if a = 0 and b ≠ 0, z = ib is purely imaginary. So every real number is a complex number.
Equality: a + ib = c + id exactly when a = c AND b = d.
Note: Im z is the real number b, not ib. For z = 3 − 5i, Im z = −5.

example.q: Find real x and y if (2x + y) + (x + 2)i = 5 + yi.

learn.reallife: AC circuit engineers write impedance as Z = R + iX (they often use j for i), with resistance as the real part and reactance as the imaginary part.

games.title: Purely real, purely imaginary or neither?

quiz.q: What is the imaginary part of z = −3 + 8i?
quiz.explain: For z = a + ib, Im z = b. Here b = 8 (a real number, without i).
quiz.mistake: Writes the imaginary part with i

quiz.q: If (x + y) + i(x − y) = 6 + 2i, where x, y are real, then x is:
quiz.explain: x + y = 6 and x − y = 2 give 2x = 8, so x = 4 (and y = 2).
quiz.mistake: Solves for y instead of x

quiz.q: Which number is purely imaginary?
quiz.explain: −5i has real part 0 and non-zero imaginary part. i² = −1 is real.
quiz.mistake: Thinks i² is imaginary because it contains i

quiz.q: Why does x² + 4 = 0 have no real solution?
options: The square of any real number is non-negative, so x² cannot equal −4
Because x must be an integer
Because 4 is not a perfect square
quiz.explain: x² ≥ 0 for real x, so x² + 4 ≥ 4 > 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the problem is with the number 4 itself

quiz.q: If 2a + 3i = 8 + (b − 1)i with a, b real, what is a + b?
quiz.explain: 2a = 8 gives a = 4; b − 1 = 3 gives b = 4. So a + b = 8.
quiz.mistake: Takes b − 1 = 3 as b = 2

quiz.q: Which statement about real and complex numbers is true?
options: Im(z) is always written with i
Every real number is a complex number
quiz.explain: A real number a can be written a + 0i, so R ⊂ C.
quiz.mistake: Thinks real and complex numbers are separate sets

quiz.q: For which real k is z = (k − 2) + (k + 3)i purely imaginary?
quiz.explain: Purely imaginary needs real part 0: k − 2 = 0, so k = 2. Then z = 5i (non-zero imaginary part).
quiz.mistake: Sets the imaginary part to 0 instead

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): i² = −1.
Reason (R): i is defined as a number whose square is −1.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: i is introduced precisely so that i² = −1, so R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Thinks i = −1

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 'imaginary numbers' are made up and useless. Explain what i is and what a complex number a + ib means.
teach.praise: i is just the number whose square is −1, and a + ib has a real part and an imaginary part. Not so imaginary after all!
teach.nudge: What is i²? And in 3 + 4i, which part is real and which is imaginary?

learn.hook: Adding complex numbers is like adding bank balances in two separate accounts — real with real, imaginary with imaginary.
points: (a + ib) + (c + id) = (a + c) + i(b + d).
Properties of addition: closure, commutative z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁, associative, additive identity 0 = 0 + 0i, additive inverse −z = −a − ib.
Subtraction: z₁ − z₂ = z₁ + (−z₂) = (a − c) + i(b − d).
Always simplify the final answer to the standard form a + ib.
Be careful with brackets: −(3 − 2i) = −3 + 2i.

example.q: Express (1/4 + 3i/4) − (2i + 3/2) in the form a + ib.

learn.reallife: Engineers add the impedances of two components in series exactly this way: real parts add and imaginary parts add.

games.title: Properties of addition
items: z₁ + z₂ = z₂ + z₁ for all complex z₁, z₂.
Real and imaginary parts are added as real numbers, which commute.
The additive identity in C is 1.
The sum of two complex numbers is always a complex number.
The additive inverse of a + ib is a − ib.
It is −a − ib; a − ib is the conjugate.
Subtraction of complex numbers is commutative.
z₁ − z₂ = −(z₂ − z₁), which differs unless z₁ = z₂.

quiz.explain: Real: 4 − 2 = 2. Imaginary: 3 + 5 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of adding

quiz.q: (3 − 2i) − (5 − 6i) equals:
quiz.explain: Real: 3 − 5 = −2. Imaginary: −2 − (−6) = 4.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to change the sign of −6i when subtracting

quiz.q: The additive inverse of −4 + 9i is:
quiz.mistake: Confuses the additive inverse with the conjugate or the reciprocal

quiz.q: If z₁ = 2 + i and z₂ = 1 − 3i, what is Re(z₁ − 2z₂)?
quiz.explain: 2z₂ = 2 − 6i. z₁ − 2z₂ = (2 − 2) + (1 + 6)i = 7i. Real part 0.
quiz.mistake: Doubles z₁ as well

quiz.q: Express (1/2 + 5i/2) + (3 + i/2) − (−3/2 + 2i) in the form a + ib.
quiz.mistake: Misses a sign when subtracting −3/2 or 2i

quiz.q: Which property is shown by (z₁ + z₂) + z₃ = z₁ + (z₂ + z₃)?
quiz.explain: Changing the grouping without changing the order is associativity.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up associative and commutative

quiz.q: If z = 5 − 2i and w = −5 + 2i, then z + w is:
quiz.explain: w = −z, so z + w = 0, the additive identity.
quiz.mistake: Adds real parts but doubles the imaginary part

quiz.explain: Imaginary parts: −3 − 2 + 7 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Treats the second bracket as being added

teach.ask: Gappu wants to add (2 + 3i) and (4 − i). Explain how to add and subtract complex numbers.
teach.praise: Real with real, imaginary with imaginary. It's like sorting socks!
teach.nudge: Which parts do you combine with which?

learn.hook: Multiply out (a + ib)(c + id) like any two brackets — then one tiny rule, i² = −1, does the magic.
points: (a + ib)(c + id) = (ac − bd) + i(ad + bc).
Properties: closure, commutative, associative, multiplicative identity 1 = 1 + 0i, and distributive z₁(z₂ + z₃) = z₁z₂ + z₁z₃.
Identities from real algebra still hold: (z₁ + z₂)² = z₁² + 2z₁z₂ + z₂², (z₁ − z₂)³ = z₁³ − 3z₁²z₂ + 3z₁z₂² − z₂³, z₁² − z₂² = (z₁ + z₂)(z₁ − z₂).
Useful results: (1 + i)² = 2i, (1 − i)² = −2i, (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b².
Always replace i² by −1 and collect real and imaginary parts at the end.
learn.reallife: Rotating a phone screen image by 90° is the same as multiplying each point (as a complex number) by i.

quiz.q: (2 + 3i)(1 − i) equals:
quiz.mistake: Takes −3i² as −3

quiz.q: What is (1 + i)⁴?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that i² = −1

quiz.q: (2 − 3i)³ equals:
quiz.mistake: Cubes each part separately

quiz.q: Which is the multiplicative identity in C?
quiz.explain: z · 1 = z for every complex z.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the additive and multiplicative identities

quiz.explain: (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² = 9 + 16 = 25, a real number.
quiz.mistake: Computes 9 − 16 = −7

steps: (a + ib)(c + id): imaginary part = ad + bc
quiz.mistake: Adds 2 and 3 without the sign of d

quiz.q: If z₁ = 2 + i and z₂ = 1 − i, then z₁² − z₂² equals:
quiz.explain: z₁² = 3 + 4i and z₂² = −2i, so z₁² − z₂² = 3 + 6i. Check: (z₁ + z₂)(z₁ − z₂) = 3 × (1 + 2i) = 3 + 6i.
quiz.mistake: Forgets (1 − i)² = −2i

quiz.q: Multiplying a complex number by i once has what effect on 3 + 2i?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 2i × i = −2

teach.ask: Gappu multiplied (3 + 2i)(4 − 5i) and got 12 − 10. Explain how to multiply complex numbers correctly.
teach.praise: Expand everything, turn i² into −1, then collect. My answer is 22 − 7i now!
teach.nudge: What happens to the i² term after you expand?

topics.title: Powers of i and roots of negative numbers

learn.hook: i, −1, −i, 1, i, −1, … The powers of i repeat every four steps — like the four seasons, or the four innings of a Test match.
points: i¹ = i, i² = −1, i³ = −i, i⁴ = 1, and then the pattern repeats.
For any integer k: i^(4k) = 1, i^(4k+1) = i, i^(4k+2) = −1, i^(4k+3) = −i. Divide the power by 4 and use the remainder.
Negative powers: 1/i = −i, so i^(−n) = 1/iⁿ. For example i^(−3) = 1/(−i) = i.
Square root of a negative real: √(−a) = i√a for a > 0, e.g. √(−9) = 3i.
√a·√b = √(ab) is FALSE when both a and b are negative: √(−4)·√(−9) = (2i)(3i) = −6, not √36 = 6.

example.q: Simplify i⁹ + i¹⁹.

learn.reallife: Digital signal processors in mobile phones use the repeating cycle 1, i, −1, −i to rotate signals in steps of 90°.

quiz.q: What is i^(−50)?
quiz.mistake: Thinks a negative power always flips the sign

quiz.q: What is i²⁰²⁶?
quiz.mistake: Uses the last digit instead of the remainder on division by 4
Multiplies under one root: √400 = 20

quiz.q: 1 + i + i² + i³ equals:
quiz.explain: 1 + i − 1 − i = 0. Any four consecutive powers of i add up to 0.
quiz.mistake: Adds the exponents

quiz.q: Simplify i^(−35) and write it in the form a + ib.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 1/(−i) = i

quiz.q: Write (i¹⁸ + i^(−25))² in the form a + ib.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the middle term 2ab when squaring

quiz.explain: √a·√b = √(ab) is not valid when both a and b are negative, so that step breaks.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the error is in i² = −1
Drops the i, or adds the last term

teach.ask: Gappu must find i⁹⁹ but can't multiply 99 times. Explain the cycle of powers of i, and warn Gappu about √(−a)·√(−b).
teach.praise: Divide by 4, use the remainder — i⁹⁹ = i³ = −i. And never merge two negative roots!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the exponent to find iⁿ quickly?

topics.title: Reciprocal and division of complex numbers

learn.hook: Dividing by 3 + 4i looks scary — until you multiply top and bottom by 3 − 4i and the i disappears from the denominator.
points: For z = a + ib ≠ 0, z·z̄ = (a + ib)(a − ib) = a² + b² = |z|², a real number.
Multiplicative inverse: z⁻¹ = 1/z = z̄/|z|² = (a − ib)/(a² + b²).
Division: z₁/z₂ = z₁ · (1/z₂) = z₁z̄₂/|z₂|², for z₂ ≠ 0.
In practice: multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the denominator.
Check: z · z⁻¹ should equal 1.

example.q: Find the multiplicative inverse of 4 − 3i.

learn.reallife: Electrical engineers find current I = V/Z by dividing a voltage by a complex impedance, using exactly this conjugate trick.

games.title: Divide (3 + 2i) by (1 − i)
items: Multiply top and bottom by 1 + i

quiz.q: The multiplicative inverse of 2 + 5i is:
quiz.mistake: Takes reciprocals of each part separately

quiz.q: (1 + i)/(1 − i) equals:
quiz.explain: Multiply by (1 + i)/(1 + i): (1 + i)²/2 = 2i/2 = i.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply the numerator by the conjugate too

quiz.q: Express (4 + √3 i)/(1 − √3 i) in the form a + ib.
quiz.explain: Multiply by 1 + √3 i: numerator 4 + 4√3 i + √3 i + 3i² = 1 + 5√3 i; denominator 1 + 3 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses 1 − 3 = −2 as the denominator

quiz.q: If z = 3 − 4i, then z·z̄ equals:
quiz.mistake: Computes a² − b²

quiz.q: What is the real part of 1/(1 − 2i)?
quiz.explain: 1/(1 − 2i) = (1 + 2i)/5, so the real part is 1/5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the imaginary part instead

quiz.q: Why do we multiply by the conjugate of the denominator when dividing?
options: Because it makes the numerator zero
Because z·z̄ is a real number, so the denominator becomes real
Because the conjugate equals the reciprocal
quiz.explain: z z̄ = a² + b² is real, removing i from the denominator.
quiz.mistake: Thinks z̄ itself is 1/z

quiz.q: Find (3 − 2i)/(2 + i) in the form a + ib.
quiz.explain: Multiply by (2 − i): numerator 6 − 3i − 4i + 2i² = 4 − 7i; denominator 5.
quiz.mistake: Takes 2i² as +2

quiz.q: What is the imaginary part of the multiplicative inverse of −i?
quiz.explain: 1/(−i) = i (multiply by i/i: i/(−i²) = i/1). So it is 0 + 1i, imaginary part 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 1/(−i) = −i

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't know how to get rid of i in the denominator of 1/(3 + 4i). Explain the conjugate trick for division.
teach.praise: Multiply by the conjugate, the bottom becomes real, and division is done. Brilliant!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply the top and bottom by, and why does it work?

learn.hook: The modulus of a complex number is its 'size' — the straight-line distance from the origin, just like how far a drone is from its launch pad.
points: For z = a + ib: modulus |z| = √(a² + b²) and conjugate z̄ = a − ib.
|z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| and |z₁/z₂| = |z₁|/|z₂| (z₂ ≠ 0).
Conjugates: (z₁ + z₂)‾ = z̄₁ + z̄₂, (z₁ − z₂)‾ = z̄₁ − z̄₂, (z₁z₂)‾ = z̄₁z̄₂, (z₁/z₂)‾ = z̄₁/z̄₂.
|z̄| = |z| and z + z̄ = 2 Re z, z − z̄ = 2i Im z.
Shortcut: to find the modulus of a product or quotient, find each modulus separately — no need to multiply out.
learn.reallife: GPS apps calculate the straight-line distance between two places with the same √(a² + b²) idea that gives the modulus.

games.title: Match the conjugate
pairs: 7 (a real number is its own conjugate)

quiz.q: The modulus of −√3 + i is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the parts instead of using the square root formula

quiz.q: The conjugate of (3 + 2i)(1 − i) is:
quiz.explain: (3 + 2i)(1 − i) = 3 − 3i + 2i + 2 = 5 − i. Its conjugate is 5 + i.
quiz.mistake: Conjugates only one factor or flips the real part

quiz.q: If |z| = 5 and |w| = 2, then |z/w| is:
quiz.mistake: Multiplies or subtracts the moduli

quiz.explain: |3 + 4i| = 5 and |1 − i| = √2, so the modulus is 5/√2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the modulus of the denominator

quiz.q: For any complex z, z + z̄ equals:
quiz.explain: (a + ib) + (a − ib) = 2a = 2 Re z.
quiz.mistake: Confuses z + z̄ with z z̄

quiz.q: If z = 2 − 3i, find |z̄|².
quiz.mistake: Uses a² − b²

quiz.q: Find the modulus of (1 + i)/(1 − i) − (1 − i)/(1 + i).
quiz.explain: (1 + i)/(1 − i) = i and (1 − i)/(1 + i) = −i, so the difference is 2i, whose modulus is 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the two fractions cancel

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): |(2 + i)(2 − i)| = 5.
Reason (R): |z₁z₂| = |z₁||z₂| for all complex z₁, z₂.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: |2 + i| = |2 − i| = √5, so the product's modulus is √5 × √5 = 5; R is the rule used.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the modulus of a product must be found by multiplying out first

teach.ask: Gappu asks: what is the 'size' of a complex number, and what is its 'mirror twin'? Explain modulus and conjugate.
teach.praise: Modulus is size, conjugate is the mirror twin. And moduli multiply nicely!
teach.nudge: How do you find |3 + 4i|, and what is the conjugate of 3 + 4i?

learn.hook: Complex numbers live on a map! Real part across, imaginary part up — and suddenly modulus is distance and conjugate is a mirror.
points: z = x + iy is plotted as the point (x, y). This plane is the complex plane or Argand plane.
The x-axis is the real axis (points a + 0i) and the y-axis is the imaginary axis (points 0 + ib). E.g. 2 + 4i is (2, 4) and −3 + i is (−3, 1) in quadrant II.
|z| = √(x² + y²) is the distance of the point (x, y) from the origin.
The conjugate z̄ = x − iy is the point (x, −y): the reflection of z in the real axis.
Syllabus note: polar form, square roots of complex numbers and complex roots of quadratic equations are not part of the current CBSE exam syllabus for this chapter.

example.q: If (x + iy)³ = u + iv, write u and v in terms of x and y, and check with x = 1, y = 2.

learn.reallife: Engineers and game designers represent 2-D positions and rotations compactly as complex numbers in a plane.

games.title: Argand plane facts
items: The conjugate of z is its reflection in the imaginary axis.
z̄ = x − iy is the reflection in the real (x) axis.
|z| is the distance of z from the origin.
Every purely imaginary number lies on the y-axis.
z and z̄ are always at the same distance from the origin.
The point for −3 − 3i lies in the second quadrant.

quiz.q: The point representing −4 + 3i in the Argand plane lies in which quadrant?
quiz.explain: (−4, 3): negative x, positive y — quadrant II.
quiz.mistake: Reads the imaginary part as the x-coordinate

quiz.q: How far is the point for 6 − 8i from the origin?
quiz.mistake: Adds or subtracts the parts directly

quiz.q: The conjugate of z = 2 + 5i is the reflection of z in:
quiz.explain: (2, 5) goes to (2, −5): a mirror image in the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Reflects in the wrong axis

quiz.q: If z = x + iy and z̄ = z, then z lies:
quiz.explain: z̄ = z means x − iy = x + iy, so y = 0: z is real.
quiz.mistake: Thinks z = z̄ forces z = 0

quiz.q: If (a + ib)(1 + i) = 2 + 4i for real a, b, then a is:
quiz.explain: (a + ib)(1 + i) = (a − b) + (a + b)i. So a − b = 2, a + b = 4, giving a = 3, b = 1.
quiz.mistake: Solves the system for b

quiz.q: If x + iy = (1 + i)/(1 − i) with x, y real, then x² + y² equals:
quiz.mistake: Takes x = y = 1

quiz.q: If z = (2 + i)², which point represents z in the Argand plane?
quiz.explain: (2 + i)² = 4 + 4i + i² = 3 + 4i, so the point is (3, 4).
quiz.mistake: Forgets i² = −1, getting (5, 4)

quiz.q: Points z, z̄, −z and −z̄ (for z = 2 + 3i) form the vertices of a:
quiz.explain: They are (2, 3), (2, −3), (−2, −3) and (−2, 3) — one point in each quadrant, forming a rectangle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks −z and z̄ are the same point

teach.ask: Gappu wants to plot −3 + 2i on graph paper. Explain the Argand plane, and what modulus and conjugate look like on it.
teach.praise: Real across, imaginary up. Modulus is distance, conjugate is a mirror image. I can draw it now!
teach.nudge: Which axis shows the imaginary part, and what does the conjugate look like on the plane?

learn.hook: You have ₹200 for samosas at ₹15 each. You can't spend MORE than you have — and that 'not more than' is an inequality: 15x ≤ 200.
points: Real life is full of limits: a budget, a speed limit, a minimum attendance. These are written as inequalities.
Two expressions compared with <, >, ≤ or ≥ form an inequality. 3 < 5 is numerical; x < 5 or 2x + 3y ≥ 6 is literal (it has variables).
Strict inequalities use < or >; slack (non-strict) ones use ≤ or ≥.
ax + b < 0 (a ≠ 0) is a linear inequality in one variable; ax + by ≥ c is linear in two variables; ax² + bx + c > 0 (a ≠ 0) is quadratic, not linear.
Turning words into symbols: 'at least' → ≥, 'at most / cannot exceed / not more than' → ≤, 'more than' → >, 'less than' → <.

example.q: Ravi earns ₹30,000 a month and spends ₹x on rent and ₹12,000 on everything else. Write the condition that his spending cannot exceed his income.
steps: 'Cannot exceed' means 'less than or equal to'.

learn.reallife: RBI's inflation target band of 4% ± 2% is an inequality: 2 ≤ inflation (%) ≤ 6.

quiz.q: Which of these is a strict inequality?
quiz.explain: Strict inequalities use > or <. The others use ≥ or ≤, which are slack.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any inequality with variables is strict

quiz.q: A cricket bat must cost at most ₹2,500. If the price is ₹p, which inequality fits?
quiz.explain: 'At most' allows equality and anything below, so p ≤ 2500.
quiz.mistake: Reads 'at most' as 'less than', excluding 2500

quiz.q: Which is a quadratic (not linear) inequality?
quiz.explain: The highest power of x is 2, so it is quadratic.
quiz.mistake: Thinks having a constant term makes it quadratic

quiz.q: 'The sum of two numbers x and y is more than 10' is written as:
quiz.explain: 'More than' means strictly greater.
quiz.mistake: Uses ≥ for 'more than'

quiz.q: Which is a numerical inequality?
quiz.explain: A numerical inequality compares only numbers, with no variables.
quiz.mistake: Confuses numerical with literal inequalities

quiz.q: A lift can carry at most 680 kg. Each person weighs about 68 kg. If x people get in, which inequality is correct?
quiz.explain: Total weight 68x must not exceed 680 kg.
quiz.mistake: Adds the weight of one person to the number of people

quiz.q: Which inequality is linear in two variables?
quiz.explain: Two variables, each with power 1 and no product term.
quiz.mistake: Counts xy as linear because each variable has power 1

quiz.q: The minimum attendance rule is 75%. Which inequality describes a student's attendance a (in %) who is allowed to sit the exam?
quiz.explain: A minimum of 75% means 75 itself is allowed, so a ≥ 75.
quiz.mistake: Excludes the boundary value 75

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't know when to use < and when to use ≤. Explain strict and slack inequalities and how to turn words like 'at least' into symbols.
teach.praise: 'At least' is ≥, 'at most' is ≤, and strict means no equality. Got it!
teach.nudge: Does 'at least 18' include 18 itself? Which sign shows that?

learn.hook: Solving an inequality is like solving an equation — with ONE trap: multiply or divide by a negative number and the sign flips.
points: A solution is a value that makes the inequality true; the set of all solutions is the solution set.
Rule 1: the same number may be added to (or subtracted from) both sides without changing the sign.
Rule 2: both sides may be multiplied or divided by the same POSITIVE number without changing the sign; for a NEGATIVE number, the sign reverses (< becomes >).
The answer depends on the allowed values: 30x < 200 gives x < 20/3, so x ∈ {1, 2, …, 6} if x ∈ N, x ∈ {…, 5, 6} if x ∈ Z, and all real x < 20/3 if x ∈ R.
With fractions, multiply through by the LCM of the denominators (a positive number) first; open brackets carefully.

example.q: Solve x/4 > x/3 + 1 for real x.
steps: Multiply by −1 and reverse the sign: x < −12.

learn.reallife: A Delhi metro card has ₹480. Each trip costs ₹40 and at least ₹100 must stay on the card: 480 − 40n ≥ 100 gives n ≤ 9.5, so at most 9 trips.

games.title: Sign rules
items: Adding the same number keeps the sign.
Dividing by −2 reverses the sign: x < −3.
Multiplying by positive 4 keeps the sign.
−x < −2, and multiplying by −1 reverses the sign.
Multiplying both sides of an inequality by 0 keeps it true and useful.
It gives 0 < 0 or 0 ≤ 0, losing all information; we only multiply by non-zero numbers.
The solutions of 4x < 20 with x ∈ N are 1, 2, 3, 4.

quiz.q: Solve −4x > 20 for real x.
quiz.explain: Divide by −4 and reverse the sign: x < −5.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to reverse the inequality when dividing by a negative number

quiz.q: How many natural numbers satisfy 18x < 100?
quiz.mistake: Rounds 5.56 up to 6

quiz.q: Solve 4x − 5 > 6x + 3 for real x.
quiz.explain: −2x > 8, then divide by −2 and flip: x < −4.
quiz.mistake: Moves terms but forgets the sign flip

quiz.q: Solve (2x − 1)/3 ≥ (3x − 2)/4 for real x.
quiz.explain: Multiply by 12: 8x − 4 ≥ 9x − 6, so −x ≥ −2 and x ≤ 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to flip the sign when dividing by −1

quiz.q: What is the largest integer x satisfying 7x − 4 < 4x + 5?
quiz.explain: 3x < 9, so x < 3. The largest integer below 3 is 2.
quiz.mistake: Includes 3 even though the inequality is strict

quiz.q: Solve 4(3 − x) ≥ 3(2 − x) for real x.
quiz.explain: 12 − 4x ≥ 6 − 3x gives 6 ≥ x.
quiz.mistake: Moves −4x across with the wrong sign

quiz.q: Which value of x is a solution of 9x + 2 < 6x + 14?
quiz.explain: 3x < 12, so x < 4. Only 3 is less than 4.
quiz.mistake: Treats x = 4 as a solution of a strict inequality

quiz.q: If x is an integer and 8x > 30, which set lists the solutions?
quiz.explain: x > 3.75, so the smallest integer solution is 4, and every larger integer works.
quiz.mistake: Includes 3 by rounding 3.75 down

teach.ask: Gappu solved −3x < 12 and wrote x < −4. Explain what went wrong and the rules for solving inequalities.
teach.praise: Divide by a negative, flip the sign! So x > −4. I'll never forget the flip now.
teach.nudge: What must happen to the sign when you divide both sides by −3?

topics.title: Number line, intervals, systems and double inequalities

learn.hook: A medicine is safe between 2 °C and 8 °C — not one, but two conditions at once. Systems and double inequalities handle exactly that.
points: On the number line, a filled (dark) circle means the end point is included (≤, ≥); a hollow circle means it is excluded (<, >).
Write answers in interval notation: x ≥ 2 → [2, ∞); x < −1 → (−∞, −1); −3 < x ≤ 5 → (−3, 5].
A system of inequalities: solve each one, then take the common part (intersection) of the solution sets.
A double inequality like a ≤ (px + q)/r ≤ b: do the same operation to all three parts; if you multiply or divide by a negative number, reverse BOTH signs.

example.q: Solve the system 2x + 1 > x − 3 and 3x − 2 ≤ 7, and write the answer as an interval.

learn.reallife: Vaccines in India's cold chain must stay between 2 °C and 8 °C: the double inequality 2 ≤ T ≤ 8, drawn as a closed segment on a thermometer.

games.title: Solve −7 ≤ 1 − 2x < 5
items: Divide all parts by −2 and reverse both signs: 4 ≥ x > −2

quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply the outer parts by 2

quiz.q: The solution x < 3 is shown on the number line by:
options: a filled circle at 3 and shading to the left
a hollow circle at 3 and shading to the left
a filled circle at 3 and shading to the right
a hollow circle at 3 and shading to the right
quiz.explain: 3 is not included (strict), and x < 3 lies to the left.
quiz.mistake: Uses a filled circle for a strict inequality

quiz.q: Solve the system x − 2 > 0 and 3x < 18.
quiz.explain: x > 2 and x < 6, so 2 < x < 6.
quiz.mistake: Divides 18 by 3 incorrectly or keeps only one inequality

quiz.q: How many integers satisfy −7 ≤ 1 − 2x < 5?
quiz.explain: This gives −2 < x ≤ 4: integers −1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.
quiz.mistake: Includes −2 or excludes 4

quiz.q: Solve the system 4x − 1 < 2(x + 5) and 2 − x/2 ≥ x − 7.
quiz.explain: First: 2x < 11 ⇒ x < 11/2. Second: × 2: 4 − x ≥ 2x − 14 ⇒ 18 ≥ 3x ⇒ x ≤ 6. Common part: x < 11/2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the union instead of the intersection

quiz.q: The interval notation for −1 ≤ x < 4 is:
quiz.explain: −1 is included → '['; 4 is excluded → ')'.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the bracket types
Stops after multiplying by 2

quiz.q: The system x > 5 and x < 2 has:
quiz.explain: No real number is both greater than 5 and less than 2, so the solution set is ∅.
quiz.mistake: Writes the gap between the numbers as the answer

teach.ask: Gappu solved −7 ≤ 1 − 2x < 5 but got the brackets wrong. Explain how to solve a double inequality and show it on a number line.
teach.praise: Treat all three parts the same, flip both signs for a negative, and draw the right dots. Neat!
teach.nudge: When you divide all three parts by −2, what happens to both inequality signs?

topics.title: Word problems: marks, integers and lengths

learn.hook: 'How much do I need in the last test to get 70% overall?' — the question every Class 11 student asks. Inequalities answer it.
points: Step 1: name the unknown. Step 2: translate the condition into an inequality. Step 3: solve. Step 4: keep only answers that make sense (whole numbers, positive lengths, etc.).
Average condition: (sum of scores)/(number of tests) ≥ target.
Consecutive odd (or even) integers: x and x + 2. Consecutive integers: x and x + 1.
Lengths: express every side or piece in terms of one variable; perimeter or total length gives the inequality.
Temperature: C = (5/9)(F − 32). A range in °F converts to a range in °C by applying the formula to both ends.

example.q: Aman scored 68 and 75 in the first two unit tests. What is the minimum he must score in the third test to have an average of at least 72?
steps: Let the third score be x.

learn.reallife: JEE and NEET aspirants use the same average-target logic when planning mock-test scores for the last few weeks.

games.title: Consecutive even integers, both > 5, sum < 23
items: Let the integers be x and x + 2 (x even)

games.title: Quick setups — find the boundary value

quiz.q: Priya's marks in two tests are 62 and 70. What is the least she must score in the third test for an average of at least 66?
quiz.mistake: Averages the two scores and stops

quiz.q: How many pairs of consecutive odd natural numbers, both greater than 6, have a sum less than 30?
quiz.mistake: Forgets that x = 13 still works because only the sum is limited

quiz.q: The longest side of a triangle is twice the shortest side, and the third side is 3 cm longer than the shortest. If the perimeter is at least 35 cm, what is the minimum length of the shortest side?
quiz.mistake: Gives the longest side instead

quiz.q: A 60 cm ribbon is cut into two pieces so that the longer piece is at least twice the shorter. What is the greatest possible length of the shorter piece?
quiz.explain: Shorter = x, longer = 60 − x ≥ 2x ⇒ x ≤ 20.
quiz.mistake: Splits the ribbon equally

quiz.q: A room's temperature must stay between 59 °F and 86 °F. Using C = (5/9)(F − 32), the range in °C is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 32 before multiplying

quiz.q: Two consecutive even positive integers x and x + 2 have a sum greater than 18, and both are less than 14. What is the smallest possible x?
quiz.explain: 2x + 2 > 18 ⇒ x > 8; x + 2 < 14 ⇒ x < 12. The even values are x = 10 only, so the smallest is 10.
quiz.mistake: Includes x = 8, which gives sum exactly 18

quiz.q: In the marks problem (a + b + x)/3 ≥ T, why do we multiply both sides by 3 without reversing the sign?
options: Because the sign always stays the same
quiz.explain: Multiplying by a positive number keeps the inequality sign; only negative numbers reverse it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sign never changes

quiz.q: A student needs at least 40 out of 100 in each of two papers and an average of at least 60. She got 48 in Paper 1. What is the least she needs in Paper 2?
quiz.explain: (48 + x)/2 ≥ 60 ⇒ x ≥ 72, which also satisfies x ≥ 40.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the 40-mark condition

teach.ask: Gappu needs a minimum score in the last test to reach an average of 75. Explain how to set up and solve such a word problem.
teach.praise: Name it, write the inequality, solve, and check it makes sense. I'll reach my 75%!
teach.nudge: What variable would you use, and which sign does 'at least' need?

learn.hook: A chemist must keep an acid solution between 6% and 8% strength. How much weaker solution can she pour in? That's a double inequality.
points: Mixture problems: amount of pure substance = concentration × volume. Track the total pure substance and the total volume.
Concentration of the mixture = (total pure substance)/(total volume); put it between the given limits.
Solve the two halves of the double inequality separately (or together), then combine.
IQ formula: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100, where MA is mental age and CA is chronological age.
If IQ lies between two values, multiply the whole inequality by CA/100 (positive) to get the range of MA.

example.q: 500 L of a 10% acid solution is mixed with x L of a 4% acid solution. For the mixture to be more than 6% but less than 8% acid, find x.

learn.reallife: Pharmacists at a Jan Aushadhi store dilute antiseptic stock solutions so the final strength stays within the safe band printed on the label.

games.title: IQ range for a 10-year-old with 90 ≤ IQ ≤ 130

items.text: Pure acid in 200 L of 15% solution = ___ L
Pure acid in x L of 5% solution = ___
Mixing 200 L and x L gives total volume ___

quiz.q: IQ = (MA/CA) × 100. For a 12-year-old, IQ lies between 75 and 125. What is the range of mental age?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by CA/100

quiz.q: A child has chronological age 8 years and mental age 10 years. What is the IQ?
quiz.mistake: Divides CA by MA instead

quiz.q: In the acid example (500 L of 10% mixed with x L of 4%), the total acid in the mixture is:
quiz.explain: 10% of 500 L is 50 L, and 4% of x L is 0.04x L.
quiz.mistake: Adds the percentages

quiz.q: 1000 L of a 12% salt solution is mixed with x L of a 2% solution to get a mixture weaker than 9%. The condition on x is:
quiz.mistake: Reverses the inequality when collecting terms

quiz.q: For IQ between 80 and 140 and CA = 15 years, what is the greatest possible mental age?
quiz.mistake: Uses the lower IQ limit

quiz.q: In mixture problems, why do we multiply both sides by (500 + x) without reversing the inequality?
options: Because the total volume 500 + x is positive
quiz.explain: Volume is always positive, so multiplying by it keeps the sign.
quiz.mistake: Thinks variables always require a sign reversal

quiz.q: A 20% solution (300 L) is mixed with x L of pure water. To keep the strength at least 12%, what is the most water that can be added?
quiz.mistake: Uses 12% of 300 only

quiz.q: Mental age range 9 ≤ MA ≤ 15 for CA = 12 corresponds to IQ:
quiz.mistake: Thinks IQ equals mental age

teach.ask: Gappu is mixing a strong and a weak juice and wants the strength between 6% and 8%. Explain how to set up a mixture inequality.
teach.praise: Track the pure stuff, divide by total volume, and squeeze it between two limits. Juice perfected!
teach.nudge: How do you find the amount of pure substance in a solution?

learn.hook: 3 kurtas and 4 pairs of jeans: how many outfits? You don't need to list them — 3 × 4 = 12. That multiplication is the most powerful idea in counting.
points: Counting by listing is slow and error-prone; the counting principles let us count arrangements and selections without listing.
Multiplication principle: if one event can happen in m ways and, after it, another can happen in n ways, the two together can happen in m × n ways.
It extends to any number of events: m × n × p × … ways.
Use it for building codes, numbers, number plates and signals position by position: fill each place in turn and multiply the choices.
Example: signals made by hoisting 2 of 4 different flags one below the other: 4 × 3 = 12 signals.

example.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if no digit is repeated?

learn.reallife: An Indian vehicle number like MH 12 AB 1234 is built position by position; the multiplication principle tells the RTO how many plates a series can issue.

items.q: 2 routes A→B, 4 routes B→C: routes A→C via B
4 flags, signals using 2 flags one below the other

games.title: Counting principle check
items: If a task has two stages with 5 and 6 ways, there are 30 ways in all.
Tossing a coin 4 times gives 8 outcomes.
The multiplication principle works for more than two events.
Multiply the number of ways for each stage.
Choosing 1 of 3 pens AND 1 of 4 pencils gives 7 ways.
Signals with 3 of 5 different flags one below another: 60.

quiz.q: A restaurant thali offers 4 choices of dal, 3 of sabzi and 2 of dessert. How many different thalis are possible?
quiz.explain: 4 × 3 × 2 = 24 by the multiplication principle.
quiz.mistake: Adds the choices instead of multiplying

quiz.q: How many outcomes are there when a coin is tossed 5 times?
quiz.explain: Each toss has 2 outcomes: 2⁵ = 32.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 2 × 5

quiz.q: How many 2-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 if digits may be repeated?
quiz.explain: Units digit must be 2 or 4 (2 ways); tens digit any of 5. 2 × 5 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the even condition and gives 25

quiz.q: A signal uses 3 of 6 different flags hoisted one below the other. How many signals are possible?
quiz.explain: 6 × 5 × 4 = 120 (a flag cannot be used twice).
quiz.mistake: Uses 6³, allowing the same flag twice

quiz.q: How many 3-digit numbers have all their digits from 1 to 9 and no digit repeated?
quiz.mistake: Allows repetition: 9³ = 729

quiz.q: From city A to B there are 3 trains, and from B to C there are 5 buses. In how many ways can Meera go from A to C via B and return to A via B, using a different train and a different bus on the way back?
quiz.explain: Going: 3 × 5 = 15. Returning with different ones: 4 × 2 = 8. Total 15 × 8 = 120.
quiz.mistake: Allows the same train and bus on the return

quiz.q: An exam has 6 true/false questions. In how many ways can a student answer all of them?
quiz.explain: 2 choices for each of 6 questions: 2⁶ = 64.
quiz.mistake: Uses 6 × 2

quiz.q: Why do we multiply, not add, the number of ways in the counting principle?
options: Because tasks happen at the same time
Because adding is only for permutations
Because multiplication gives a bigger number
Each way of doing the first task can be combined with every way of doing the second
quiz.explain: For each of the m choices there are n follow-ups, giving m groups of n, i.e. m × n.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the rule is arbitrary

teach.ask: Gappu has 3 caps and 4 scarves and wants to know how many combos he can wear. Explain the fundamental principle of counting.
teach.praise: For every cap, 4 scarves: 3 × 4 = 12 looks. I'm the best-dressed bird in the sky!
teach.nudge: Why do we multiply 3 by 4 and not add them?

learn.hook: A 4-digit UPI PIN can repeat digits; a lucky-draw ticket with all-different digits cannot. That one rule changes the count completely.
points: With repetition allowed, every position has the full number of choices: 4-digit PINs from 0–9 = 10⁴ = 10,000.
Without repetition, the choices drop by one at each step: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040.
Fill restricted positions FIRST (e.g. the units digit for even numbers, the first digit that cannot be 0).
Words from letters: 'word' means any arrangement of letters, with or without meaning.
Example: 4-letter codes from the first 10 letters of the alphabet without repetition: 10 × 9 × 8 × 7 = 5040.

example.q: How many 4-digit even numbers can be formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
steps: Units digit: 2 or 4 → 2 choices (fill it first).

learn.reallife: Mobile numbers in India have 10 digits starting with 6, 7, 8 or 9 — counting with repetition explains why TRAI never runs out quickly.

games.title: Repetition allowed or not?
items: Answer key of an MCQ test

items.q: 4-letter words from A, B, C, D, E, repetition allowed

quiz.q: How many 3-digit numbers can be formed from the digits 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 with no digit repeated?
quiz.explain: First digit cannot be 0: 4 choices; then 4 remaining for tens (including 0) and 3 for units. 4 × 4 × 3 = 48.
quiz.mistake: Allows 0 in the hundreds place

quiz.q: How many 4-letter codes can be made from the first 8 letters of the English alphabet without repetition?
quiz.mistake: Uses 8⁴, allowing repetition

quiz.q: 6-digit phone numbers in a town all begin with 98 and use the digits 0–9 with no digit repeated. How many such numbers are possible?
quiz.explain: After 9 and 8, 8 digits remain for 4 places: 8 × 7 × 6 × 5 = 1680.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that 9 and 8 are already used

quiz.q: How many 3-digit odd numbers can be formed using 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 if repetition is allowed?
quiz.explain: Units digit odd: 1, 3, 5 (3 ways); hundreds and tens: 6 each. 3 × 6 × 6 = 108.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the odd condition: 216

quiz.q: How many 5-letter 'words' (with or without meaning) can be formed from the letters of DELHI with no letter repeated?
quiz.mistake: Allows repetition: 5⁵

quiz.q: In how many ways can 3 different prizes be given to 5 students if a student may win more than one prize?
quiz.explain: Each prize can go to any of 5 students: 5³ = 125.
quiz.mistake: Uses 5 × 4 × 3, assuming no student wins twice

quiz.q: How many numbers between 100 and 1000 can be formed using 1, 3, 5, 7 if repetition is allowed?
quiz.explain: Such numbers have 3 digits, each from 4 choices: 4³ = 64.
quiz.mistake: Forbids repetition

quiz.q: To count 3-digit even numbers from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition, which place should be filled first?
options: It does not matter at all
quiz.explain: The units place carries the restriction (must be 2 or 4); filling it first avoids double counting.
quiz.mistake: Fills the restricted place last and over-counts

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't know why 4-digit PINs are 10,000 but 4-digit codes with different digits are only 5040. Explain the difference.
teach.praise: With repetition every place has 10 choices; without it, the choices shrink. Mystery solved!
teach.nudge: What happens to the number of choices for the next place when digits cannot repeat?

learn.hook: In how many ways can 11 players walk out in a line before a World Cup match? 11! = 39,916,800. Factorials grow FAST.
points: A permutation is an arrangement of objects in a definite order.
Number of permutations of n different objects taken r at a time (no repetition): nPr = n(n − 1)(n − 2)…(n − r + 1) = n!/(n − r)!, 0 ≤ r ≤ n.
Derivation: fill r places one by one — n choices, then n − 1, …, then n − r + 1 — and multiply.
With repetition allowed, the number of arrangements of n objects taken r at a time is nʳ.

example.q: Evaluate 8!/(6! × 2!).

learn.reallife: The BCCI's selection panel ranking 3 players for 'captain, vice-captain, wicketkeeper' from 15 is ¹⁵P₃ = 2730 ordered choices.

games.title: Derive nPr = n!/(n − r)!
items: First place can be filled in n ways
Second place in (n − 1) ways, …, r-th place in (n − r + 1) ways

quiz.q: Evaluate ⁷P₃.
quiz.mistake: Computes 7C3 = 35

quiz.q: What is the value of 0! + 1!?
quiz.explain: 0! = 1 by definition and 1! = 1, so the sum is 2.
quiz.mistake: Thinks 0! = 0

quiz.explain: 3! + 4! = 6 + 24 = 30, while 7! = 5040. Factorials do not add like this.
quiz.mistake: Assumes (a + b)! = a! + b!

quiz.q: In how many ways can 4 different books be arranged on a shelf from a collection of 9 different books?
quiz.mistake: Uses combinations or 9⁴
Keeps only one of the terms

quiz.q: How many 3-letter codes can be made from 26 letters if repetition is allowed?
quiz.mistake: Uses ²⁶P₃ = 15,600 (no repetition)

quiz.q: The value of n!/(n − 2)! is:
quiz.mistake: Cancels only one factor

quiz.q: Evaluate n!/(r!(n − r)!) for n = 6, r = 2.
quiz.mistake: Forgets r! in the denominator, getting 30

teach.ask: Gappu thinks 0! should be 0 and that 3! + 4! = 7!. Explain factorials and the formula for nPr.
teach.praise: 0! is 1, factorials don't add, and nPr = n!/(n − r)!. My counting is sharper now!
teach.nudge: What is 0! defined to be, and why?

learn.hook: Swap the two Os in 'BALLOON' and nothing changes. That's why arrangements of alike letters need dividing, not just multiplying.
points: If p of n objects are alike (and the rest different), the number of arrangements of all n is n!/p!.
Reason: swapping the p alike objects among themselves (p! ways) gives the same arrangement, so n! counts each one p! times.
If p₁, p₂, …, pₖ objects are alike of k kinds, the number of arrangements is n!/(p₁! p₂! … pₖ!).
Example: MISSISSIPPI has 11 letters with I × 4, S × 4, P × 2: 11!/(4! 4! 2!) = 34,650.
ALLAHABAD has 9 letters with A × 4, L × 2: 9!/(4! 2!) = 7560.

example.q: How many different words can be formed from the letters of BALLOON?
steps: 7 letters: B, A, L, L, O, O, N.
L appears 2 times, O appears 2 times.

learn.reallife: A DNA sequence of 10 bases with 4 A, 3 G, 2 C and 1 T can be arranged in 10!/(4! 3! 2! 1!) = 12,600 ways — biotech labs count exactly like this.

items.text: Arrangements of n objects, p alike = n!/___

quiz.q: How many distinct arrangements of the letters of BANANA are there?
quiz.mistake: Divides only by 3!

quiz.q: How many different words can be made from the letters of COMMITTEE?
quiz.mistake: Divides by only one or two of the 2!s

quiz.q: In how many ways can 3 red, 2 blue and 1 green ball (balls of the same colour identical) be arranged in a row?
quiz.mistake: Treats all balls as different

quiz.q: How many arrangements of the letters of ALLAHABAD are there?
quiz.explain: 9 letters: A × 4, L × 2, others single. 9!/(4! 2!) = 7560.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2! for the Ls

quiz.q: Why do we divide by p! when p objects are alike?
options: Because permuting the alike objects among themselves gives no new arrangement
Because alike objects cannot be arranged
quiz.explain: Each distinct arrangement is counted p! times in n!, once for each order of the alike objects.
quiz.mistake: Thinks alike objects are simply removed

quiz.q: How many 4-digit numbers can be formed using the digits 1, 1, 2, 2 (each used once)?
quiz.mistake: Treats the repeated digits as different

quiz.q: How many distinct words can be made with the letters of MISSISSIPPI?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 2! for the two Ps

quiz.q: The letters of LEVEL are arranged in all possible ways. How many arrangements are there?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2! only once

teach.ask: Gappu counts the words from BANANA as 720. Explain why that is too many and how to correct it.
teach.praise: Swapping the As doesn't make a new word, so divide by 3! and 2!. Only 60 words!
teach.nudge: If you swap two As in BANANA, do you get a new word?

learn.hook: 'Vowels must sit together', 'the number must be divisible by 5' — exam questions love conditions. The trick: handle the condition first.
points: Vowels together: glue them into one block, arrange the block with the other letters, then arrange the vowels inside the block.
Vowels never together = (all arrangements) − (arrangements with all vowels together), when the condition is 'not all together'.
Fixed positions: if a word must start or end with given letters, place them first, then arrange the rest.
Divisibility: even → last digit even; divisible by 5 → last digit 0 or 5; divisible by 10 → last digit 0. Fill that place first.
To find n from a relation like nP5 = 20 nP3, write both sides as products and cancel: (n − 3)(n − 4) = 20, so n = 8.

example.q: In how many arrangements of the letters of DAUGHTER are the vowels together? In how many are they not all together?
steps: DAUGHTER has 8 different letters; vowels A, U, E.
Glue the vowels: 5 consonants + 1 block = 6 units → 6! = 720.

learn.reallife: Seating plans at a wedding ('keep the family of the bride together') are vowels-together problems in disguise.

games.title: Arrangements of MONDAY starting with M and ending with Y
items: Fix M in the first place and Y in the last place
Letters left for the middle: O, N, D, A

items.q: Words from MONDAY starting with M
Words from 4 different letters, a given letter first
4-digit numbers from 1–5, no repetition, divisible by 5
Arrange 3 boys and 2 girls in a row, girls together

quiz.q: Find n if ⁿP₄ = 12 × ⁿP₂.
quiz.mistake: Solves (n − 2)(n − 3) = 12 as n = 5

quiz.q: Find n if ⁿP₅ = 20 × ⁿP₃.
quiz.mistake: Expands incorrectly and takes n = 9

quiz.q: How many 4-digit numbers divisible by 10 can be formed from 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 without repetition?
quiz.explain: Units digit must be 0. The other 3 places come from 5 digits: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to fix the last digit as 0

quiz.q: In how many arrangements of the letters of EQUATION do all the vowels occur together?
quiz.explain: Vowels E, U, A, I, O form one block; with Q, T, N that is 4 units → 4! = 24. Inside the block 5! = 120. Total 24 × 120 = 2880.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to arrange the vowels within the block

quiz.q: In how many arrangements of DAUGHTER are the vowels NOT all together?
quiz.explain: Total 8! = 40320 minus together 6! × 3! = 4320 gives 36,000.
quiz.mistake: Gives the 'together' count

quiz.q: How many 3-digit even numbers can be formed from 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7 with no repetition?
quiz.explain: Units digit from 2, 4, 6 (3 ways); then 5 and 4 for the other places: 3 × 5 × 4 = 60.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the even condition

quiz.q: How many words can be made from the letters of MONDAY using all letters, if the word must start with a vowel?
quiz.explain: Vowels are O and A (2 choices for the first place); the remaining 5 letters: 5! = 120. 2 × 120 = 240.
quiz.mistake: Counts only one vowel

quiz.q: In how many ways can 4 boys and 3 girls stand in a row if the girls occupy the even places (2nd, 4th, 6th)?
quiz.explain: Girls in the 3 even places: 3! = 6; boys in the 4 odd places: 4! = 24. 6 × 24 = 144.
quiz.mistake: Adds instead of multiplies, or ignores the condition

teach.ask: Gappu wants the number of arrangements of DAUGHTER with vowels together. Explain the 'glue the block' trick and how to get 'not together'.
teach.praise: Glue, arrange, unglue — and subtract for 'not together'. That's a neat trick!
teach.nudge: After gluing the vowels into a block, what else must you multiply by?

learn.hook: Choosing 3 friends for a trip to Goa is a combination — the order you pick them doesn't matter. Ranking them 1st, 2nd, 3rd would be a permutation.
points: A combination is a selection where order does not matter.
nCr = n!/(r!(n − r)!), 0 ≤ r ≤ n. Each selection of r objects can be arranged in r! ways, so nPr = r! × nCr.
nC0 = nCn = 1, and nCr = nC(n − r) (choosing r to take = choosing n − r to leave).
If nCa = nCb, then a = b or a + b = n.
Pascal's rule: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr.

example.q: If ⁿC₇ = ⁿC₅, find ⁿC₂.

learn.reallife: A cricket selector picking 15 players from 25 probables for a squad is choosing a combination: ²⁵C₁₅ = 3,268,760 squads are possible.

games.title: Permutation or combination?
items: Choosing 3 books to take on a trip
Electing a president and a secretary

quiz.q: Evaluate ¹⁰C₃.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 3!, giving ¹⁰P₃ = 720

quiz.q: If ⁿC₂ = 45, then n is:
quiz.mistake: Solves n(n − 1) = 45

quiz.q: If ⁿC₁₀ = ⁿC₆, then ⁿC₂ is:
quiz.mistake: Takes n = 10 − 6 = 4

quiz.q: Using Pascal's rule, ⁸C₅ + ⁸C₄ equals:
quiz.explain: nCr + nC(r − 1) = (n + 1)Cr with n = 8, r = 5 gives ⁹C₅.
quiz.mistake: Adds the upper and lower numbers

quiz.q: If ⁿP_r = 720 and ⁿC_r = 120, then r is:
quiz.mistake: Takes r = 6 from r! = 6

quiz.q: Which is equal to ²⁰C₁₇?
quiz.explain: nCr = nC(n − r): ²⁰C₁₇ = ²⁰C₃.
quiz.mistake: Confuses nCr with nPr

quiz.q: In how many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 9 people?
quiz.explain: ⁹C₃ = (9 × 8 × 7)/6 = 84. Order does not matter in a committee.
quiz.mistake: Uses ⁹P₃ = 504

quiz.q: If ²ⁿC₃ : ⁿC₃ = 11 : 1, then n is:
quiz.mistake: Cancels incorrectly and gets n = 11

teach.ask: Gappu thinks choosing 3 friends and ranking 3 friends give the same count. Explain combinations, nCr and how it links to nPr.
teach.praise: Selecting ignores order, so divide the permutations by r!. Team picking made easy!
teach.nudge: If order does not matter, why do we divide nPr by r!?

learn.hook: The school quiz team needs 2 boys and 3 girls, with at least one Class 12 student. Questions like this mix combinations with 'at least' and 'at most'.
points: Separate groups: choose from each group and multiply, e.g. 2 boys from 7 and 3 girls from 5: ⁷C₂ × ⁵C₃.
'At least' / 'at most': add the cases, or use total − unwanted cases (e.g. at least 1 girl = total − no girls).
Cards: a deck has 52 cards, 4 suits of 13, 4 aces, 12 face cards (J, Q, K). Exactly one ace in 4 cards: ⁴C₁ × ⁴⁸C₃.
Lines through n points (no three collinear): ⁿC₂. Triangles: ⁿC₃. Diagonals of an n-gon: ⁿC₂ − n.
Read 'exactly', 'at least' and 'at most' carefully — they decide which cases to add.

example.q: A committee of 5 is to be formed from 6 boys and 5 girls with exactly 3 boys and 2 girls. In how many ways?

learn.reallife: A Ranji Trophy squad selection ('at least 4 bowlers, at most 2 wicket-keepers') is solved with exactly these case-by-case combinations.

games.title: At least 1 girl in a team of 3 from 5 boys and 4 girls
items: Use the complement: at least 1 girl = total − teams with no girl
Subtract the no-girl teams (⁵C₃ = 10) from this total

quiz.q: In how many ways can a team of 3 boys and 2 girls be chosen from 7 boys and 5 girls?
quiz.mistake: Adds the two counts

quiz.q: From 5 boys and 4 girls, how many teams of 3 have at least one girl?
quiz.explain: Total ⁹C₃ = 84; teams with no girls ⁵C₃ = 10. 84 − 10 = 74.
quiz.mistake: Counts only teams with exactly one girl

quiz.q: In how many ways can 4 cards be drawn from a deck of 52 so that exactly one is an ace?
quiz.explain: Choose the ace: ⁴C₁ = 4. Choose 3 non-aces from 48: ⁴⁸C₃ = 17,296. 4 × 17,296 = 69,184.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to choose which ace

quiz.q: In how many ways can 4 cards of the same suit be chosen from a deck?
quiz.explain: Choose the suit (4 ways) and 4 of its 13 cards: 4 × ¹³C₄ = 4 × 715 = 2860.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to multiply by the 4 suits

quiz.q: How many triangles can be formed using 12 points in a plane, no three of which are collinear?
quiz.mistake: Uses ¹²C₂ (lines) or ¹²P₃

quiz.q: How many diagonals does an octagon have?
quiz.explain: ⁸C₂ − 8 = 28 − 8 = 20 (remove the 8 sides).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract the sides

quiz.q: A student must answer 7 of 10 questions, choosing at least 3 from the first 5. In how many ways can she choose? (She can take 3, 4 or 5 from the first group.)
quiz.explain: 3 from first: ⁵C₃ × ⁵C₄ = 50; 4: ⁵C₄ × ⁵C₃ = 50; 5: ⁵C₅ × ⁵C₂ = 10. Total 110.
quiz.mistake: Misses the case of all 5 from the first group

quiz.q: In how many ways can a hand of 4 cards be all face cards?
quiz.explain: There are 12 face cards; ¹²C₄ = 495.
quiz.mistake: Uses 16 'picture' cards including aces

teach.ask: Gappu must pick a team with 'at least one girl' and is counting case by case. Show a faster way and explain how to handle 'at least' and 'at most'.
teach.praise: Total minus the unwanted case — so quick! And for 'at most', add the allowed cases.
teach.nudge: Instead of adding many cases, what could you subtract from the total?

learn.hook: Make 5-letter words from DAUGHTER using 2 vowels and 3 consonants: first CHOOSE the letters, then ARRANGE them. Most hard problems are two easy ones glued together.
points: Mixed problems: number of ways = (ways to select) × (ways to arrange the selected objects).
Example: 2 vowels from 3 and 3 consonants from 5 in DAUGHTER, then arrange 5 letters: ³C₂ × ⁵C₃ × 5! = 3600.
Dictionary (rank) problems: list letters alphabetically; count words that begin with each smaller letter, then fix letters one by one.
Rows with restrictions: place the restricted group first (e.g. girls in even places), then the rest.
Always check whether letters are distinct; repeated letters need division by factorials.

example.q: If all arrangements of RANK are listed in dictionary order, what is the rank of RANK?
steps: Letters in order: A, K, N, R.
Words starting with A, K, N: 3 × 3! = 18.
Starting with R: next letter A; remaining K, N give RAKN (19th), RANK (20th).

learn.reallife: Password-strength meters estimate how many passwords an attacker must try — select characters, then arrange them.

games.title: Rank of MOTHER in dictionary order
items: Letters: E, H, M, O, R, T
MO then E, H or R: 3 × 3! = 18
MOT then E: 2! = 2; next MOTHER itself

items.q: Choose 3 of 5 people, seat in a row
2 vowels of 3 and 1 consonant of 4, arrange
Choose 2 of 5 books, arrange on shelf
Rank of CAT among arrangements of A, C, T

quiz.q: How many 5-letter words with 2 different vowels and 3 different consonants can be formed from the letters of DAUGHTER?
quiz.explain: Choose vowels ³C₂ = 3, consonants ⁵C₃ = 10, arrange 5 letters 5! = 120. 3 × 10 × 120 = 3600.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to arrange the chosen letters

quiz.q: The letters of LEMON are arranged in dictionary order. What is the rank of LEMON?
quiz.explain: Order: E, L, M, N, O. Starting with E: 24. L then E: LE + arrangements of M, N, O; LEMNO is 25th, LEMON is 26th.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1 for the word itself

quiz.q: How many 4-letter words can be formed from 6 different letters if each word must have 2 specific letters? (Choose 2 more from the other 4, then arrange.)
quiz.mistake: Forgets to arrange the 4 letters

quiz.q: In how many ways can 3 boys be chosen from 6 and seated in a row of 3 chairs?
quiz.mistake: Stops at the selection

quiz.q: Rank of the word ACT among all arrangements of A, C, T in dictionary order:
quiz.explain: ACT is the first word: A, then C, then T in alphabetical order.
quiz.mistake: Counts words before it instead of its position

quiz.q: How many 3-digit numbers with distinct digits can be formed by choosing 2 odd digits from 1, 3, 5 and 1 even digit from 2, 4?
quiz.mistake: Forgets one of the selection steps

quiz.q: In how many ways can 2 Physics and 2 Chemistry books be chosen from 4 Physics and 3 Chemistry books (all different) and placed on a shelf?
quiz.explain: ⁴C₂ × ³C₂ = 6 × 3 = 18 selections; each can be arranged in 4! = 24 ways. 18 × 24 = 432.
quiz.mistake: Stops at 18 without arranging

quiz.q: Why is the rank of a word found by counting words that come BEFORE it and adding 1?
options: Because every word is counted twice
Because its position is one more than the number of words ahead of it
Because the last letter is fixed
quiz.explain: If k words come earlier, the word is in position k + 1.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add 1 for the word itself

teach.ask: Gappu must form words with 2 vowels and 3 consonants and then find a word's dictionary rank. Explain 'select then arrange' and how ranking works.
teach.praise: Pick first, then arrange — and count the words before mine for its rank. Chirpy clear!
teach.nudge: After choosing the letters, what is the next step?

topics.title: Patterns in powers and Pascal's triangle

learn.hook: Can you find 98⁵ without multiplying 98 by itself five times? A triangle of numbers known in India as Meru Prastaara, centuries before Pascal, makes it easy.
points: Repeated multiplication of big powers like (98)⁵ or (a + b)ⁿ is slow; we want a formula.
(a + b)⁰ = 1, (a + b)¹ = a + b, (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b², (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³, (a + b)⁴ = a⁴ + 4a³b + 6a²b² + 4ab³ + b⁴.
The coefficients form Pascal's triangle: each row starts and ends with 1, and every inner entry is the sum of the two entries just above it.
The entries of row n are ⁿC₀, ⁿC₁, …, ⁿCₙ — Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ is exactly 'add the two above'.

example.q: Use Pascal's triangle to expand (a + b)⁵.
steps: Powers of a fall 5 → 0; powers of b rise 0 → 5.

learn.reallife: Counting Sanskrit verse metres in Pingala's Chhandaḥśāstra led to this pattern; the commentator Halayudha (10th century CE) described it as Meru Prastaara, long before Pascal.

games.title: Build row 6 of Pascal's triangle
games.prompt: Rows in order, top to bottom

games.title: Entry ↔ nCr
pairs: Last entry of any row n

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of a²b² in (a + b)⁴?
quiz.explain: Row 4 of Pascal's triangle is 1, 4, 6, 4, 1; the middle term is 6a²b².
quiz.mistake: Uses the power 4 as the coefficient

quiz.q: In Pascal's triangle, the entry below 10 and 10 in row 5 is:
quiz.explain: Each entry is the sum of the two above it: 10 + 10 = 20 (the middle of row 6).
quiz.mistake: Multiplies instead of adds

quiz.q: Which row of Pascal's triangle gives the coefficients of (x + y)⁶?
quiz.explain: Row 6 (counting the top 1 as row 0) has 7 entries: 1, 6, 15, 20, 15, 6, 1.
quiz.mistake: Picks row 5 or invents a pattern

quiz.q: What is the sum of the entries in row 5 of Pascal's triangle?
quiz.mistake: Forgets one of the end 1s

quiz.q: Which expression gives the 3rd entry of row 7 in Pascal's triangle?
quiz.explain: Entries of row 7 are ⁷C₀, ⁷C₁, ⁷C₂, …, so the 3rd entry is ⁷C₂ = 21.
quiz.mistake: Starts counting from ⁷C₁

quiz.q: The coefficients in (a + b)³ are:
quiz.explain: (a + b)³ = a³ + 3a²b + 3ab² + b³.
quiz.mistake: Uses row 2

quiz.q: Pascal's rule ⁿCᵣ + ⁿCᵣ₋₁ = ⁿ⁺¹Cᵣ corresponds to which feature of Pascal's triangle?
options: Each row has one more entry than the previous
Each entry is the sum of the two entries above it
quiz.explain: The two entries above position r in row n + 1 are ⁿCᵣ₋₁ and ⁿCᵣ.
quiz.mistake: Links the rule to symmetry instead

quiz.q: How many entries are there in row 9 of Pascal's triangle?
quiz.explain: Row n has n + 1 entries (ⁿC₀ to ⁿCₙ).
quiz.mistake: Counts n entries

teach.ask: Gappu wants to write row 6 of Pascal's triangle from memory. Explain how the triangle is built and how it links to (a + b)ⁿ.
teach.praise: Add the two above, put 1s at the ends, and you get the coefficients of (a + b)ⁿ. Triangle power!
teach.nudge: How do you get an inside number of Pascal's triangle from the row above?

learn.hook: One formula expands (a + b)ⁿ for every positive integer n — no matter how big. That's the binomial theorem.
points: (a + b)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ aⁿ + ⁿC₁ aⁿ⁻¹ b + ⁿC₂ aⁿ⁻² b² + … + ⁿCₙ bⁿ, for any positive integer n.
Why: (a + b)ⁿ is n brackets multiplied. A term aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ appears once for every way of choosing b from r of the n brackets — ⁿCᵣ ways.
There are n + 1 terms. Powers of a fall from n to 0, powers of b rise from 0 to n, and in each term the indices add up to n.
The numbers ⁿCᵣ are the binomial coefficients; they read the same from both ends because ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
Syllabus note: the general-term and middle-term formulas are not part of the current CBSE syllabus for this chapter.

example.q: Expand (x + 2)⁴ using the binomial theorem.

learn.reallife: Actuaries at LIC use binomial expansions to estimate probabilities of many independent events, like several policies maturing together.

games.title: Why the coefficient of aⁿ⁻ʳbʳ is ⁿCᵣ
items: Write (a + b)ⁿ as n brackets (a + b)(a + b)…(a + b)
Each term comes from picking a or b from every bracket
To get aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, pick b from exactly r brackets
This can be done in ⁿCᵣ ways
So the term is ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ

games.title: Facts about (a + b)ⁿ
items: In every term, the powers of a and b add up to n.
The coefficients read the same from both ends.
The first term of (a + b)ⁿ is ⁿC₁ aⁿ.
The first term is ⁿC₀ aⁿ = aⁿ.

quiz.q: How many terms are there in the expansion of (2x + 3y)⁹?
quiz.explain: (a + b)ⁿ has n + 1 terms, so 9 + 1 = 10.
quiz.mistake: Counts n terms

quiz.q: The coefficient of x³ in (x + 1)⁵ is:
quiz.explain: The term is ⁵C₂ x³ (1)² = 10x³.
quiz.mistake: Uses ⁵C₁

quiz.q: In (a + b)⁷, the term containing a³ also contains:
quiz.explain: The powers add to 7, so a³ goes with b⁴.
quiz.mistake: Makes the powers equal

quiz.q: The expansion of (x + 3)³ is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to raise 3 to the right powers

quiz.q: The coefficient of a²b⁴ in (a + b)⁶ is:
quiz.explain: ⁶C₄ = ⁶C₂ = 15.
quiz.mistake: Takes the power of b as the coefficient

quiz.q: Which is the correct statement of the binomial theorem for positive integer n?
options: (a + b)ⁿ = Σ ⁿCᵣ aⁿ⁻ʳ bʳ, r = 0 to n
quiz.explain: Coefficients are combinations, powers of a fall and powers of b rise.
quiz.mistake: Uses permutations or equal powers

quiz.q: In the expansion of (x + 2)⁴, what is the coefficient of x²?
quiz.explain: ⁴C₂ x² (2)² = 6 × 4 x² = 24x².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square 2

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The coefficient of a²b³ in (a + b)⁵ equals the coefficient of a³b².
Reason (R): ⁿCᵣ = ⁿCₙ₋ᵣ.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: a²b³ has coefficient ⁵C₃ and a³b² has ⁵C₂; these are equal by the symmetry rule R.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coefficients depend on which letter is first

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know why the coefficient of a³b² in (a + b)⁵ is ⁵C₂. Explain the binomial theorem and the counting reason behind it.
teach.praise: Pick b from 2 of the 5 brackets — ⁵C₂ ways. The theorem is just counting!
teach.nudge: From how many brackets do you choose b to get b² in (a + b)⁵?

learn.hook: Put a minus sign in (x − y)ⁿ and the signs start alternating: + − + − … Spot that and expansions become automatic.
points: (x − y)ⁿ = ⁿC₀xⁿ − ⁿC₁xⁿ⁻¹y + ⁿC₂xⁿ⁻²y² − … + (−1)ⁿ ⁿCₙ yⁿ: signs alternate.
(1 + x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² + … + ⁿCₙxⁿ and (1 − x)ⁿ = ⁿC₀ − ⁿC₁x + ⁿC₂x² − … + (−1)ⁿ ⁿCₙxⁿ.
Put x = 1 in (1 + x)ⁿ: ⁿC₀ + ⁿC₁ + … + ⁿCₙ = 2ⁿ. The sum of the coefficients of any expansion = its value at x = 1.
For terms like (x² + 3/x)⁴, write a = x², b = 3/x and simplify powers carefully: (3/x)² = 9/x².

example.q: Expand (x + 2/x)⁴ and find the term independent of x.

learn.reallife: Engineers use (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x — e.g. a 1% expansion of a rail track repeated over many segments.

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of x³ in (1 − 2x)⁵?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the minus sign from (−2)³

quiz.q: The sum ⁷C₀ + ⁷C₁ + … + ⁷C₇ equals:
quiz.explain: The sum of all binomial coefficients of (1 + x)⁷ is 2⁷ = 128.
quiz.mistake: Uses 7²

quiz.q: What is the constant term in the expansion of (x − 1/x)⁶?
quiz.explain: The x⁰ term needs x³ · (−1/x)³: ⁶C₃ (−1)³ = −20.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the alternating sign

quiz.q: Which is the expansion of (x − y)⁴?
quiz.explain: Signs alternate starting with +; the y⁴ term has (−1)⁴ = +1.
quiz.mistake: Makes every term after the first negative

quiz.q: The coefficient of x² in (2x − 3)⁴ is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square both 2 and −3

quiz.q: What is the sum of the coefficients in (3x − 2)⁵?
quiz.mistake: Adds only the positive coefficients

quiz.q: In the expansion of (x² + 3/x)⁴, which term contains x²?
quiz.explain: ⁴C₂ (x²)² (3/x)² = 6 × x⁴ × 9/x² = 54x².
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the 3

quiz.q: (1 + x)ⁿ − (1 − x)ⁿ contains only:
quiz.explain: Even-power terms have the same sign in both and cancel; odd-power terms double.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the even powers survive

teach.ask: Gappu expanded (x − 2)³ and made every term negative. Explain the sign pattern in (x − y)ⁿ and how to find the sum of the coefficients.
teach.praise: Signs flip-flop: + − + −. And x = 1 gives the sum of the coefficients. Easy!
teach.nudge: Which terms of (x − y)ⁿ get a minus sign?

topics.title: Using the theorem: big powers, comparisons, divisibility

learn.hook: 96³ in your head? Write it as (100 − 4)³ and the binomial theorem does it in four easy terms.
points: Write the base near a round number: 96 = 100 − 4, 101 = 100 + 1, 0.98 = 1 − 0.02.
Comparisons: (1.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ = (1 + 0.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ = 1 + 1000000 × 0.01 + (positive terms) > 1 + 10000 > 10000.
Divisibility: write the base as 1 + k. Then (1 + k)ⁿ = 1 + nk + k²(…), so (1 + k)ⁿ − nk − 1 is a multiple of k².
Example: 6ⁿ = (1 + 5)ⁿ = 1 + 5n + 25(…), so 6ⁿ − 5n leaves remainder 1 on division by 25.

example.q: Show that 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 is divisible by 64 for every positive integer n.

learn.reallife: Bank interest compounding, (1 + r)ⁿ, is approximated by 1 + nr + ⁿC₂r² — quick mental maths for loan officers.

games.title: Write the base as round number ± small

quiz.q: Using (100 − 1)⁴, find 99⁴.
quiz.mistake: Gets a sign wrong in the alternating terms

quiz.q: Using the binomial theorem, (0.98)³ equals:
quiz.mistake: Stops after the first two terms

quiz.q: Which is larger, (1.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ or 10000?
options: Cannot be decided without a calculator
quiz.explain: (1 + 0.01)¹⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰⁰ > 1 + 1000000 × 0.01 = 10001 > 10000, since the other terms are positive.
quiz.mistake: Thinks powers of a number close to 1 stay close to 1

quiz.q: What is the remainder when 7ⁿ − 6n is divided by 36, for any positive integer n?
quiz.mistake: Thinks the expression is an exact multiple of 36

quiz.q: Which expression shows 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 is divisible by 64?
quiz.explain: After removing 1 and 8n, every remaining term of (1 + 8)ⁿ has a factor 8² = 64.
quiz.mistake: Stops at a factor of 8

quiz.q: Using (2 − 0.1)², compute (1.9)².
quiz.mistake: Forgets the middle term or its sign

quiz.q: Find (102)³ using the binomial theorem.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square or cube the 2

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): 6ⁿ − 5n leaves remainder 1 when divided by 25, for every positive integer n.
Reason (R): 6ⁿ = (1 + 5)ⁿ = 1 + 5n + 25 × (an integer).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Subtracting 5n from R gives 6ⁿ − 5n = 1 + 25k, which is exactly A.
quiz.mistake: Does not see that R directly proves A

teach.ask: Gappu must compute 99⁴ without a calculator and prove 9ⁿ − 8n − 1 is divisible by 64. Explain the trick of writing the base as 'round ± small'.
teach.praise: 99 = 100 − 1, expand, and the big powers are easy. Same trick proves divisibility. Wow!
teach.nudge: How can you write 99 using a nice round number?

learn.hook: (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴ looks messy — but add the two expansions and half the terms vanish, leaving a whole number.
points: (a + b)ⁿ + (a − b)ⁿ = 2[terms with even powers of b]; (a + b)ⁿ − (a − b)ⁿ = 2[terms with odd powers of b].
To find n and a from given terms: compare coefficients, e.g. if (1 + ax)ⁿ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + …, then na = 8 and ⁿC₂ a² = 24.
Trinomials: group two terms as one, e.g. (1 + x + x²)² = ((1 + x) + x²)², then expand twice.
Always simplify surds at the end: (√2)⁴ = 4, (√3)³ = 3√3.

example.q: Evaluate (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴.
steps: Odd-power terms cancel; even-power terms double.

learn.reallife: Signal-processing engineers combine (a + b)ⁿ and (a − b)ⁿ to isolate even or odd parts of a signal.

games.title: Find n and a if (1 + ax)ⁿ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + …
Surd expansions
items: Odd powers of 1 with √2 terms cancel; the result is 34.
(a + b)⁵ − (a − b)⁵ contains the term a⁵.
a⁵ appears in both with the same sign and cancels.
Expanding ((1 + x) + x²)² gives exactly this.
The coefficient of x³ in (1 + x + x²)³ is 6.

quiz.q: Evaluate (√3 + 1)⁴ − (√3 − 1)⁴.
quiz.explain: Only odd powers of 1 survive, doubled: 2[⁴C₁(√3)³ + ⁴C₃(√3)] = 2[12√3 + 4√3] = 32√3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double

quiz.q: Evaluate (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to double the surviving terms

quiz.q: If (1 + ax)ⁿ = 1 + 8x + 24x² + …, then n is:
quiz.explain: na = 8 gives n²a² = 64, and n(n − 1)a²/2 = 24 gives n(n − 1)a² = 48. Dividing: (n − 1)/n = 3/4, so n = 4 and a = 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes n = 8 from the coefficient of x

quiz.q: What is the coefficient of x³ in (1 + x + x²)³?
quiz.explain: Ways to make x³ from three factors: (x, x, x) → 1 way; (1, x, x²) in any order → 6 ways. Total 7.
quiz.mistake: Misses the x·x·x choice

quiz.q: (a + b)⁶ + (a − b)⁶ contains which powers of b?
options: Only even powers: b⁰, b², b⁴, b⁶
quiz.explain: Odd-power terms have opposite signs in the two expansions and cancel.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the odd terms survive

quiz.q: Expand (1 + x + x²)² by grouping as ((1 + x) + x²)². The coefficient of x² is:
quiz.explain: (1 + x)² + 2(1 + x)x² + x⁴ = 1 + 2x + x² + 2x² + 2x³ + x⁴, so x² has 1 + 2 = 3.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the cross term 2(1 + x)x²

quiz.q: If the coefficients of x and x² in (1 + x)ⁿ are equal, then n is:
