quiz.mistake: Uses ⁿC₁ = ⁿC₀

quiz.q: What is the value of (x + 1)³ + (x − 1)³ at x = 2?
quiz.mistake: Doubles only x³

teach.ask: Gappu must evaluate (√2 + 1)⁴ + (√2 − 1)⁴ without expanding fully twice. Explain the add-and-cancel shortcut.
teach.praise: Add them and the odd terms vanish — just double the rest. A whole number pops out!
teach.nudge: When you add (a + b)ⁿ and (a − b)ⁿ, which terms disappear?

learn.hook: India's population year by year, your SIP balance month by month, a phone's value after each year of use — all are sequences.
points: A sequence is an ordered list of numbers a₁, a₂, a₃, …; aₙ is the nth term or general term.
A finite sequence has a last term (e.g. the marks in 5 unit tests); an infinite sequence goes on forever (e.g. 1, 1/2, 1/3, …).
Formally, a sequence is a function whose domain is N (or {1, 2, …, k} for a finite one): n ↦ aₙ.
Some sequences are given by a recurrence: earlier terms define later ones.
Fibonacci sequence: a₁ = a₂ = 1, aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + aₙ₋₂ for n > 2: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, …

example.q: Write the first five terms of aₙ = n(n + 3).

learn.reallife: The Fibonacci numbers show up in sunflower seed spirals and pine cones — and in the counting of Sanskrit metres studied by Virahanka and Hemachandra long before Fibonacci.

games.title: Fibonacci terms
games.prompt: Grow the sequence one term at a time (shortest list first)

quiz.q: If aₙ = (n − 1)/(n + 1), what is a₄?
quiz.mistake: Substitutes n = 4 only in the numerator

quiz.q: What is the 6th term of the Fibonacci sequence 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, …?
quiz.explain: Each term is the sum of the two before: 3 + 5 = 8.
quiz.mistake: Adds 1 each time

quiz.q: A sequence has a₁ = 2 and aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 1 for n > 1. What is a₃?
quiz.mistake: Stops at a₂ or uses a₁ again

quiz.q: Which describes a sequence most precisely?
options: A function whose domain is R
A function whose domain is the set of natural numbers (or a part of it starting at 1)
quiz.explain: The position n ∈ N is the input and the term aₙ is the output.
quiz.mistake: Confuses a sequence with a series or a set

quiz.q: If aₙ = n²/3ⁿ, what is a₄?
quiz.mistake: Multiplies 3 × 4 instead of raising 3 to the power 4

quiz.q: Which sequence is infinite?
options: The sequence of all odd natural numbers
The scores of 11 batters in an innings
quiz.explain: Odd natural numbers 1, 3, 5, … never end.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a long list must be infinite

quiz.q: For aₙ = (−1)ⁿ 2ⁿ⁺¹, what is a₃?
quiz.mistake: Takes (−1)³ as +1, or uses 2³

quiz.q: If a₁ = 1 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 2, what is a₅?
quiz.mistake: Counts one term too many

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what 'nth term' means and how the Fibonacci sequence works. Explain sequences and recurrences.
teach.praise: A list in order, a rule for the nth term, and sometimes a rule using earlier terms. Fibo-fantastic!
teach.nudge: How do you get the next Fibonacci number from the ones before it?

learn.hook: Adding the terms of a sequence gives a series — like adding up your monthly pocket money to get the year's total.
points: If a₁, a₂, a₃, … is a sequence, then a₁ + a₂ + a₃ + … is the corresponding series.
A series is finite or infinite according as the sequence is finite or infinite.
Sigma notation: Σₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖ means a₁ + a₂ + … + aₙ. Here k is the index, 1 and n are the limits.
Example: Σₖ₌₁⁴ k² = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 = 30.
To find terms from a formula, substitute n = 1, 2, 3, …; from a recurrence, build up one term at a time.

example.q: Write the first five terms of a₁ = 2, aₙ = aₙ₋₁/n (n ≥ 2), and write the corresponding series.

learn.reallife: A company's annual report adds 12 monthly revenues — Σ from k = 1 to 12 of Rₖ — to get yearly turnover.

quiz.q: Evaluate Σₖ₌₁⁵ k².
quiz.mistake: Squares the sum 15 instead of summing squares

quiz.q: Which is the difference between a sequence and a series?
options: A series is the sum of the terms of a sequence
quiz.explain: The sequence lists terms; the series adds them.
quiz.mistake: Uses the two words interchangeably

quiz.q: Σₖ₌₁⁴ (3k + 1) equals:
quiz.mistake: Adds only one +1

quiz.q: With a₁ = a₂ = 3 and aₙ = aₙ₋₁ − 2 for n > 2, what is the sum of the first five terms?
quiz.mistake: Starts subtracting from a₁ instead of a₂

quiz.q: The series 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + 1/8 + … is:
quiz.explain: It has no last term, so it is an infinite series.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a series with a finite total must be finite

quiz.q: Write 3 + 6 + 9 + … + 30 in sigma notation.
quiz.explain: The terms are 3k for k = 1 to 10 (3 × 10 = 30).
quiz.mistake: Uses the last term as the upper limit

quiz.q: If aₙ = 2n + 1, what is a₁ + a₂ + a₃?
quiz.mistake: Adds the indices instead of the terms

quiz.q: In Σₖ₌₁ⁿ aₖ, the letter k is called the:
quiz.explain: k runs from the lower limit 1 to the upper limit n.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the index with the limits

teach.ask: Gappu sees Σ and freezes. Explain what a series is and how to read sigma notation.
teach.praise: Σ just means 'add these up', with k running from bottom to top. Not scary at all!
teach.nudge: What does the little k under Σ do, and where does it stop?

learn.hook: One bacterium becomes 2, then 4, then 8 … In a GP each term is the previous one multiplied by the same number — and the numbers explode.
points: A G.P. is a sequence in which each term (after the first) is a fixed non-zero multiple of the previous one: aₖ₊₁/aₖ = r, the common ratio.
With first term a: a, ar, ar², ar³, …; the nth term is aₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
To find unknowns, write two given terms as arᵖ⁻¹ and arᑫ⁻¹ and divide to find r, then substitute to find a.
Three numbers in G.P. are best taken as a/r, a, ar (product a³); four as a/r³, a/r, ar, ar³.
If r > 1 (and a > 0) the terms grow; if 0 < r < 1 they shrink; if r < 0 the signs alternate.

example.q: Which term of the G.P. 3, 3√3, 9, … is 729?

learn.reallife: Computer memory sizes 1 KB, 2 KB, 4 KB, 8 KB … double each step — a G.P. with r = 2.

games.title: GP or not?
items: Each term is 3 times the previous one.
The common ratio of a G.P. can be 0.
r must be non-zero; otherwise the terms after the first are 0.
Each term is one-third of the previous one.

quiz.q: Find the 8th term of the G.P. 5, 10, 20, …
quiz.mistake: Uses rⁿ instead of rⁿ⁻¹

quiz.q: The 4th term of a G.P. is 24 and the 7th term is 192. What is the common ratio?
quiz.mistake: Takes r = 8 without the cube root

quiz.q: In the G.P. above (a₄ = 24, a₇ = 192), the first term is:
quiz.explain: ar³ = 24 with r = 2 gives 8a = 24, so a = 3.
quiz.mistake: Divides 24 by 2 only once

quiz.q: Three numbers in G.P. have product 216 and sum 21. What are they?
quiz.mistake: Picks numbers with the right product but wrong sum

quiz.q: Which term of the G.P. 3, 6, 12, … is 768?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the n − 1 in the exponent

quiz.q: The 5th term of the G.P. 1/2, −1, 2, … is:
quiz.mistake: Gets the sign of (−2)⁴ wrong

quiz.q: If x, 2x + 2, 3x + 3 are in G.P., then x is:
quiz.mistake: Accepts x = −1, which gives zero terms

quiz.q: If a, b, c are in G.P., which is always true?
quiz.explain: b/a = c/b ⇒ b² = ac.
quiz.mistake: Uses the AP condition 2b = a + c

teach.ask: Gappu's savings grow by 10% every year and he wants the amount in year 6. Explain what a G.P. is and its nth-term formula.
must: a r to the n minus 1
teach.praise: Multiply by r each time; the nth term is a·rⁿ⁻¹. My savings plan is ready!
teach.nudge: What do you multiply by to get from one term to the next?

topics.title: Sum of a G.P. and special series

learn.hook: The legend of the chessboard: 1 grain on square 1, 2 on square 2, 4 on square 3, … The total on 64 squares is 2⁶⁴ − 1 — more rice than India grows in centuries!
points: Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1) = a(1 − rⁿ)/(1 − r) for r ≠ 1. If r = 1, Sₙ = na.
Derivation: write Sₙ and rSₙ, subtract: (r − 1)Sₙ = arⁿ − a.
Series like 0.3 + 0.03 + 0.003 + … are G.P.s with r = 1/10.
5 + 55 + 555 + … to n terms: write each term as (5/9)(10ᵏ − 1); the sum is (5/81)(10ⁿ⁺¹ − 9n − 10).
Infinite G.P. with |r| < 1 (formative, for awareness): the sum approaches a/(1 − r). E.g. 1 + 1/2 + 1/4 + … = 2.

example.q: Find the sum of the first 8 terms of 3 + 6 + 12 + …

learn.reallife: An EMI or SIP schedule with a fixed growth rate adds up as a G.P.; financial calculators at banks use Sₙ = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1).

quiz.q: Find the sum of the first 6 terms of the G.P. 2, 6, 18, …
quiz.mistake: Uses 3⁵ instead of 3⁶

quiz.q: The sum of the G.P. 1 − 1/2 + 1/4 − 1/8 + … to 6 terms is:
quiz.mistake: Ignores the negative ratio

quiz.q: What is the sum to n terms of 0.3 + 0.03 + 0.003 + …?
quiz.mistake: Adds the terms as if they were equal

quiz.q: The sum to n terms of 5 + 55 + 555 + … is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −1 in each term

quiz.q: How many terms of the G.P. 2, 2², 2³, … are needed to give the sum 126?
quiz.mistake: Divides 126 by 2 and stops

quiz.q: The sum of the infinite G.P. 6 + 3 + 3/2 + … is:
quiz.mistake: Thinks an infinite series must have an infinite sum

quiz.q: If the sum of n terms of a G.P. with a = 1 and r = 1 is 15, then n is:
quiz.explain: When r = 1, every term is a, so Sₙ = na = n = 15.
quiz.mistake: Applies the formula with r − 1 = 0

quiz.q: In the legend, the number of grains on all 64 squares of a chessboard (1, 2, 4, …) is:
quiz.mistake: Gives the grains on the last square only

teach.ask: Gappu wants the total of 1 + 2 + 4 + … for 20 terms without adding them one by one. Explain the G.P. sum formula and why it works.
teach.praise: Multiply by r, subtract, and nearly everything cancels. 2²⁰ − 1 grains it is!
teach.nudge: What happens when you subtract Sₙ from rSₙ?

learn.hook: Average of 4 and 16? The everyday average says 10. The geometric mean says 8. Both are useful — and they are always in the same order.
points: Arithmetic mean of a and b: A = (a + b)/2, so a, A, b are in A.P.
Geometric mean of positive a and b: G = √(ab), so a, G, b are in G.P.
Inserting n geometric means G₁, …, Gₙ between a and b makes a G.P. of n + 2 terms: b = arⁿ⁺¹, so r = (b/a)^(1/(n + 1)).
Example: 3 G.M.s between 1 and 256: r⁴ = 256, r = 4: 4, 16, 64.
The G.M. of 4 and 9 is 6; the A.M. is 6.5.

example.q: Insert two geometric means between 3 and 81.

learn.reallife: Economists use the geometric mean to average growth rates — a GDP growth of 10% then −10% averages out below zero, not to zero.

quiz.q: What is the geometric mean of 3 and 27?
quiz.mistake: Gives the arithmetic mean 15

quiz.q: What is the arithmetic mean of 7 and 19?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2

quiz.q: Insert three geometric means between 2 and 32. The middle one is:
quiz.explain: r⁴ = 32/2 = 16 ⇒ r = 2: 2, 4, 8, 16, 32. The middle mean is 8.
quiz.mistake: Uses r³ = 16

quiz.q: If 4 geometric means are inserted between 1/3 and 81, what is the common ratio?
quiz.mistake: Uses r⁴ for 4 means

quiz.q: The geometric mean of 2 and 8 is:
quiz.mistake: Adds and halves

quiz.q: If the G.M. of x and 16 is 8, then x is:
quiz.mistake: Halves 8

quiz.q: Between which pair of numbers is the A.M. equal to the G.M.?
quiz.explain: A = G only when the numbers are equal. For 4 and 9: A = 6.5, G = 6.
quiz.mistake: Thinks A = G for any pair of squares

quiz.q: How many terms does the G.P. have after inserting n geometric means between a and b?
quiz.explain: The two given numbers a and b plus the n means make n + 2 terms.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to include a and b

teach.ask: Gappu wants the 'middle' number between 4 and 16 in a G.P. Explain arithmetic and geometric means and how to insert G.M.s.
teach.praise: A.M. adds and halves, G.M. multiplies and roots. Inserting means is just finding r!
teach.nudge: To insert n means between a and b, how many terms does the G.P. have?

topics.title: G.P. in real life and G.P. proofs

learn.hook: Bacteria in a lab, money in a fixed deposit, the value of a used scooter — they all multiply by the same factor each period.
points: Growth: P, Pk, Pk², … with k > 1 (e.g. bacteria tripling: k = 3).
Compound interest: ₹P at r% per year becomes P(1 + r/100)ⁿ after n years — the (n + 1)th term of a G.P.
Depreciation at r% per year: value after n years = P(1 − r/100)ⁿ.
Ancestors: 2 parents, 4 grandparents, 8 great-grandparents, … (assuming no common ancestors).
Proof idea: to show x, y, z are in G.P., show y² = xz (or y/x = z/y). E.g. if a, b, c are in G.P. then b² = ac, so (b²)² = a²c², and a², b², c² are in G.P.

example.q: A culture starts with 50 bacteria, and the number triples every hour. How many are there after 4 hours?

learn.reallife: A car bought for ₹8,00,000 that loses 20% of its value each year is worth 8,00,000 × (0.8)³ = ₹4,09,600 after 3 years — used-car dealers apply this formula every day.

games.title: Model ↔ formula
pairs: ₹P at r% compound interest, n years
Value after r% depreciation, n years
Ancestors in the kth generation back
Test for x, y, z in G.P.

games.title: Prove: if a, b, c, d are in G.P., then ab, bc, cd are in G.P.
items: Let the common ratio be r: b = ar, c = ar², d = ar³
ab = a²r, bc = a²r³, cd = a²r⁵
Equal ratios, so ab, bc, cd are in G.P.

quiz.q: ₹1000 is deposited at 10% per year compound interest. What is the amount after 3 years?
quiz.mistake: Uses simple interest

quiz.q: A scooter worth ₹60,000 depreciates by 10% every year. What is its value after 2 years?
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 10% of the original value each year

quiz.q: Counting parents, grandparents and so on (no common ancestors), how many ancestors does a person have in the previous 5 generations?
quiz.mistake: Counts only the 5th generation

quiz.q: A bacteria culture doubles every hour. If there are 3200 after 5 hours, how many were there at the start?
quiz.mistake: Divides by 2 × 5 = 10

quiz.q: If a, b, c are in G.P., which of these triples is also always in G.P.?
options: a + b, b + c, c + a
quiz.explain: b² = ac ⇒ (b²)² = a²c², so a², b², c² are in G.P.
quiz.mistake: Thinks adding a constant keeps a G.P.

quiz.q: If 1, x, 9 are in G.P. with x > 0, then x is:
quiz.mistake: Uses the A.M. 5

quiz.q: A ball dropped from 81 m rebounds to 2/3 of its height each time. How high does it rise after the 3rd bounce?
quiz.mistake: Stops after 2 bounces (36 m)

quiz.q: The population of a town grows by 5% per year from 20,000. Which expression gives the population after 6 years?
quiz.explain: Each year multiplies by 1.05, six times.
quiz.mistake: Treats compound growth as simple growth

teach.ask: Gappu's grandfather put ₹1000 in a bank at 10% compound interest. Explain why the yearly amounts form a G.P. and how to prove three numbers are in G.P.
teach.praise: Each year multiplies by 1.1 — that's a G.P.! And b² = ac proves it. Grandpa will be proud.
teach.nudge: What do you check to prove x, y, z are in G.P.?

learn.hook: For any two positive numbers, the arithmetic mean is never smaller than the geometric mean. This tiny fact solves optimisation puzzles from fencing to packaging.
points: For positive a and b: A = (a + b)/2 and G = √(ab).
Proof: A − G = (a + b)/2 − √(ab) = (√a − √b)²/2 ≥ 0. So A ≥ G, with equality exactly when a = b.
Given A and G, the numbers are the roots of x² − 2Ax + G² = 0, i.e. A ± √(A² − G²).
Ratio problems: if A : G is given, write a and b in terms of √a and √b, or use a + b = 2A and ab = G².
For a G.P. of n terms with sum S, product P and sum of reciprocals R: P²Rⁿ = Sⁿ.

example.q: The A.M. and G.M. of two positive numbers are 10 and 8. Find the numbers.
steps: They are the roots of x² − 20x + 64 = 0.

learn.reallife: A farmer near Nashik fencing a rectangular field with 100 m of wire gets the largest area by making it a square — AM ≥ GM says xy ≤ ((x + y)/2)².

games.title: Prove A ≥ G
items: A square is never negative, so A − G ≥ 0

games.title: A.M. vs G.M.
items: For 2 and 8, A = 5 and G = 4, so A > G.
A.M. can be less than G.M. for some positive numbers.
A = G when the two numbers are equal.
If A = 13 and G = 12, the numbers are 18 and 8.
a + b = 26, ab = 144: roots of x² − 26x + 144 = 0 are 18 and 8.
A.M. ≥ G.M. holds for negative numbers too.
The result is stated for positive numbers; √(ab) may not even be real otherwise.

quiz.q: The A.M. of two positive numbers is 25 and their G.M. is 20. What is the larger number?
quiz.mistake: Doubles the G.M.

quiz.q: Which expression equals A − G for positive a, b?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the square roots

quiz.q: If the ratio A.M. : G.M. of two positive numbers is 5 : 4, then the numbers are in the ratio:
quiz.explain: Let a + b = 10k, √(ab) = 4k ⇒ ab = 16k². a, b = 8k, 2k, ratio 4 : 1. (Check 4 and 1: A = 2.5, G = 2.)
quiz.mistake: Copies the ratio of the means

quiz.q: For positive x, what is the least value of x + 9/x?
quiz.explain: AM ≥ GM: (x + 9/x)/2 ≥ √9 = 3, so x + 9/x ≥ 6, reached at x = 3.
quiz.mistake: Takes the least value as 9

quiz.q: The A.M. and G.M. of two numbers are 15 and 9. What is their product?
quiz.explain: G² = ab = 81.
quiz.mistake: Uses A² = 225

quiz.q: Two positive numbers have sum 26 and G.M. 5. What is the smaller number?
quiz.mistake: Takes the G.M. as one of the numbers

quiz.q: In a G.P. of n terms, S is the sum, P the product and R the sum of reciprocals. Which relation holds?
quiz.explain: With S = a(rⁿ − 1)/(r − 1), P = aⁿr^(n(n−1)/2) and R = (rⁿ − 1)/(a rⁿ⁻¹(r − 1)), one checks P²Rⁿ = Sⁿ.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square P

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For positive a and b, (a + b)/2 ≥ √(ab).
Reason (R): (√a − √b)² ≥ 0 for all positive a, b.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Expanding R gives a + b ≥ 2√(ab), which is A. So R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the square with the inequality

teach.ask: Gappu doesn't believe the A.M. is always at least the G.M. Prove it and show how to find two numbers from their A.M. and G.M.
teach.praise: A perfect square can't be negative, so A ≥ G. And the numbers come out of a quadratic. Convinced!
teach.nudge: Why is (√a − √b)² never negative, and what does that tell us?

topics.title: Coordinate recall and slope of a line

learn.hook: Indian Railways signs say 'gradient 1 in 100' on the ghats — that is a slope. Coordinate geometry turns such steepness into a single number m.
points: Recall: distance PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²); internal section point ((mx₂ + nx₁)/(m + n), (my₂ + ny₁)/(m + n)); triangle area = ½|x₁(y₂ − y₃) + x₂(y₃ − y₁) + x₃(y₁ − y₂)|.
Coordinate geometry links algebra and geometry: a line becomes an equation, and geometric facts become calculations.
The inclination θ of a line is the angle it makes with the positive x-axis, measured anticlockwise, 0° ≤ θ < 180°.
Slope m = tan θ (θ ≠ 90°). A horizontal line has m = 0; the slope of a vertical line is not defined.
Through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂), x₁ ≠ x₂: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁).

example.q: Find the slope of the line through (3, −2) and (−1, 4), and say whether its inclination is acute or obtuse.
steps: A negative slope means tan θ < 0, so 90° < θ < 180°.

learn.reallife: A railway gradient board reading '1 in 100' means the track rises 1 m for every 100 m — a slope of 1/100.

quiz.q: What is the slope of a line inclined at 30° to the positive x-axis?
quiz.mistake: Uses sin 30° instead of tan 30°

quiz.q: Find the slope of the line through (−2, 3) and (4, −6).
quiz.mistake: Puts the x-difference on top

quiz.q: A line has slope −1. What is its inclination?
quiz.explain: tan θ = −1 with 0° ≤ θ < 180° gives θ = 135°.
quiz.mistake: Gives a negative angle or one outside [0°, 180°)

quiz.q: The slope of the line through (5, 1) and (5, 7) is:
quiz.explain: x₂ − x₁ = 0, so the line is vertical and its slope is not defined.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a vertical line has slope 0

quiz.q: The distance between (2, −1) and (−4, 7) is:
quiz.mistake: Adds the differences instead of squaring

quiz.q: The point dividing the segment from (1, 2) to (7, 8) internally in the ratio 1 : 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Swaps m and n and gets (5, 6)

quiz.q: Using slopes, are A(1, 1), B(2, 3), C(4, 7) collinear?
options: Yes, because they have positive coordinates
quiz.explain: Slope AB = (3 − 1)/(2 − 1) = 2 and slope BC = (7 − 3)/(4 − 2) = 2; equal slopes through a common point B means collinear.
quiz.mistake: Compares coordinates instead of slopes

quiz.q: If the line through (k, 3) and (2, 7) has slope 2, then k is:
quiz.mistake: Solves 4/(2 − k) = 2 as k = 4

teach.ask: Gappu thinks a vertical cliff has slope 0 because 'it doesn't go anywhere sideways'. Explain inclination and slope.
teach.praise: Slope is rise over run, tan θ — and a vertical line has no defined slope. Cliff confusion over!
teach.nudge: What is the 'run' for a vertical line, and what goes wrong when you divide by it?

learn.hook: Railway tracks never meet: equal slopes. A road crossing them at a level crossing makes a right angle: slopes multiply to −1.
points: Two non-vertical lines are parallel exactly when their slopes are equal: m₁ = m₂.
Two non-vertical lines are perpendicular exactly when m₁m₂ = −1 (slopes are negative reciprocals).
A horizontal line (m = 0) is perpendicular to every vertical line.
Three points A, B, C are collinear exactly when slope AB = slope BC.
A linear relation between two quantities (cost and units, °C and °F) has a straight-line graph; its slope is the rate of change.

example.q: Using slopes, show that A(0, 0), B(2, 2), C(3, −3) form a right triangle.

learn.reallife: Hostel fees: ₹50,000 for 0 extra months and ₹62,000 for 3 extra months fit the line F = 4000m + 50,000; the slope ₹4000 per month is the rate of change.

games.title: Slope relationships
items: Lines with slopes 3 and −1/3 are perpendicular.
Lines with slopes 2 and −2 are perpendicular.
If slope AB = slope BC, then A, B, C are collinear.
Same slope and a common point B means the same line.
Two lines with slopes 0 and 0 can be perpendicular.
Both are horizontal, so they are parallel.

quiz.q: A line is perpendicular to a line of slope 3/4. What is its slope?
quiz.mistake: Takes the reciprocal but forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: The line through (−1, 2) and (2, 8) is perpendicular to the line through (4, 5) and (x, 1). Find x.
quiz.explain: First slope = 6/3 = 2, so the second slope must be −1/2: (1 − 5)/(x − 4) = −1/2 ⇒ x − 4 = 8 ⇒ x = 12.
quiz.mistake: Sets the slopes equal (parallel) instead

quiz.q: If A(0, 0), B(4, 1), C(6, 4), D(2, 3) are joined in order, which pairs of sides are parallel?
quiz.explain: Slope AB = 1/4 = slope DC; slope BC = 3/2 = slope AD. So ABCD is a parallelogram.
quiz.mistake: Compares adjacent sides instead of opposite ones

quiz.q: For what k are the points (1, 2), (3, 6) and (k, 10) collinear?
quiz.mistake: Uses the wrong pair of points

quiz.q: A taxi charges ₹100 for 5 km and ₹180 for 15 km, following a straight line. What is the charge per km (the slope)?
quiz.mistake: Divides 180 by 15

quiz.q: In the taxi example above, what is the fixed charge (the value at 0 km)?
quiz.explain: C = 8d + c with 100 = 40 + c, so c = 60.
quiz.mistake: Takes the 5 km charge as the fixed charge

quiz.q: Lines with slopes m and −1/m (m ≠ 0) are:
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative slopes make lines parallel

quiz.q: Which pair of lines is parallel?
quiz.explain: 4x − 2y = 7 gives y = 2x − 7/2, slope 2, same as y = 2x + 3.
quiz.mistake: Compares the constants instead of the slopes

teach.ask: Gappu wants to check if two roads are parallel or meet at right angles using only slopes. Explain the conditions.
teach.praise: Equal slopes — parallel; product −1 — perpendicular. Road planning sorted!
teach.nudge: What must the product of the slopes be for perpendicular lines?

learn.hook: Two runways at an airport cross at an angle; air-traffic engineers compute it straight from the slopes.
points: If lines have slopes m₁ and m₂ (1 + m₁m₂ ≠ 0), the acute angle θ between them satisfies tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)|.
The obtuse angle between them is 180° − θ.
If 1 + m₁m₂ = 0, the lines are perpendicular (θ = 90°).
To find an unknown slope from the angle, remove the modulus: (m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂) = ± tan θ, giving two answers.

example.q: The angle between two lines is π/4 and one slope is 1/3. Find the other slope.

learn.reallife: Crossing runways at an airport such as Mumbai's are set at an angle to suit the wind; the angle comes straight from their slopes.

games.title: Find the acute angle between slopes 2 and −3

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between lines with slopes √3 and 1/√3.
quiz.explain: These lines are inclined at 60° and 30°, so the angle between them is 30°. (tan θ = |(√3 − 1/√3)/(1 + 1)| = 1/√3.)
quiz.mistake: Adds the inclinations

quiz.q: For lines with slopes m₁ and m₂, the lines are perpendicular when:
quiz.explain: Then the formula's denominator is 0, tan θ is undefined and θ = 90°.
quiz.mistake: Uses m₁ + m₂ = 0

quiz.q: What is tan θ for the acute angle between y = 2x + 1 and y = 3x − 4?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the 1 in the denominator

quiz.q: The acute angle between two lines is 45° and one slope is 2. Which pair gives all possible values of the other slope?
quiz.mistake: Drops the modulus and keeps only one case

quiz.q: The obtuse angle between two lines whose acute angle is 50° is:
quiz.explain: The angles between two crossing lines are θ and 180° − θ.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts from 90° or 360°

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between the x-axis and the line through (0, 0) and (1, √3).
quiz.explain: Slope √3 = tan 60°, and the x-axis has slope 0.
quiz.mistake: Uses cot instead of tan

quiz.q: Lines have slopes 3 and −1/2. tan of the acute angle between them is:
quiz.mistake: Gets the reciprocal by swapping numerator and denominator

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The formula tan θ = |(m₂ − m₁)/(1 + m₁m₂)| gives the acute angle between two lines.
Reason (R): The modulus makes tan θ non-negative.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A non-negative tangent corresponds to an angle in [0°, 90°), i.e. the acute (or zero) angle; that is why the modulus is used.
quiz.mistake: Does not link the modulus to choosing the acute angle

teach.ask: Gappu needs the angle between two lines with slopes 1/2 and 3. Explain the formula and why it has a modulus sign.
teach.praise: Difference over one-plus-product, with a modulus for the acute angle. 45° it is!
teach.nudge: What does the modulus do to the value of tan θ?

learn.hook: Give a GPS one point and a direction, or two points, and it can draw your road. Those are the point-slope and two-point forms.
points: Horizontal line through (a, b): y = b. Vertical line through (a, b): x = a. The x-axis is y = 0 and the y-axis is x = 0.
Point-slope form: the line through (x₀, y₀) with slope m is y − y₀ = m(x − x₀).
Two-point form: through (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂): y − y₁ = [(y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)](x − x₁).
A point lies on a line exactly when its coordinates satisfy the equation.
Simplify to the form Ax + By + C = 0 for the final answer.

example.q: Find the equation of the line through (−2, 3) with slope −4.

learn.reallife: Delhi Metro planners describe a straight track segment between two stations by the two-point form using the stations' map coordinates.

quiz.q: The equation of the line through (3, −2) with slope 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses y − 2 instead of y + 2

quiz.q: The line through (1, 2) and (−3, 4) is:
quiz.mistake: Gets the slope sign wrong

quiz.q: Which is the equation of the vertical line through (−4, 7)?
quiz.explain: Every point on a vertical line has the same x-coordinate.
quiz.mistake: Confuses vertical and horizontal

quiz.q: Does the point (2, 1) lie on 3x − 4y − 2 = 0?
quiz.explain: Substituting gives 0, so the point satisfies the equation.
quiz.mistake: Makes an arithmetic slip when substituting

quiz.q: The line through (0, 0) and (−2, 6) is:
quiz.mistake: Drops the negative sign of the slope

quiz.q: A line passes through (2, 3) and has inclination 45°. Its equation is:
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the sign when moving terms

quiz.q: For what value of k does the line through (1, k) and (3, 7) also pass through (5, 11)?
quiz.mistake: Uses the slope 4 between y-values

quiz.q: The y-coordinate of the point on the line through (1, 1) and (4, 7) with x = 3 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses slope 3

teach.ask: Gappu knows one point on a road and its slope. Explain how to write the road's equation, and how to do it with two points instead.
teach.praise: One point plus slope, or two points — find the slope and plug in. Roads drawn!
teach.nudge: If you have two points, what do you calculate first?

learn.hook: Your phone bill = fixed rental + rate × minutes: y = mx + c. The fixed part is the intercept, the rate is the slope.
points: Slope-intercept form: y = mx + c, where c is the y-intercept (the line meets the y-axis at (0, c)).
With x-intercept d: y = m(x − d).
Intercept form: x/a + y/b = 1 meets the x-axis at (a, 0) and the y-axis at (0, b).
From Ax + By + C = 0 (B ≠ 0): slope = −A/B and y-intercept = −C/B; for C ≠ 0, x-intercept = −C/A and y-intercept = −C/B.
Real data: if price p and demand d are linearly related, two data points give the line, and it predicts other values.

example.q: Reduce 3x + 4y − 12 = 0 to slope-intercept and intercept forms.

learn.reallife: A Pune dairy sells 1000 L of milk a day at ₹40/L and 900 L at ₹45/L. Assuming a linear relation, it predicts sales of 800 L at ₹50/L.

items.text: x + 7y = 0 in slope form: y = ___ x

quiz.q: Find the slope and y-intercept of 6x + 3y − 5 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide the constant by 3

quiz.q: The line with x-intercept 3 and y-intercept −2 is:
quiz.mistake: Swaps the intercepts or drops the minus sign

quiz.q: The line through (−3, 5) that cuts off equal intercepts on the axes is:
quiz.explain: x/a + y/a = 1 ⇒ x + y = a. Substitute: −3 + 5 = 2 = a.
quiz.mistake: Uses x − y for equal intercepts

quiz.q: What is the x-intercept of 3x − 4y + 12 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Puts x = 0 and finds the y-intercept

quiz.q: A dairy sells 1000 L of milk a day at ₹40/L and 900 L at ₹45/L. Assuming a linear relation, how much will it sell at ₹50/L?
quiz.mistake: Takes the change of 100 L per ₹1 instead of per ₹5

quiz.q: The line y = mx + c passes through (1, 4) and (3, 10). What is c?
quiz.mistake: Confuses c with m

quiz.q: Which equation has slope −3/2 and y-intercept 4?
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the coefficients of x and y

quiz.q: A rod's length L (cm) depends linearly on temperature T (°C): L = 120.04 at 10 °C and 120.24 at 60 °C. By how many cm does it grow per °C?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by the 50 °C change

teach.ask: Gappu's phone plan costs ₹199 fixed plus ₹1 per minute. Explain y = mx + c and the intercept form x/a + y/b = 1.
teach.praise: Slope is the rate, intercept is the fixed part, and x/a + y/b = 1 shows where the axes are cut. Bill decoded!
teach.nudge: In y = mx + c, which letter is the fixed starting value?

topics.title: Lines in triangles; parallel and perpendicular lines through a point

learn.hook: Every triangle hides special lines — medians, altitudes, perpendicular bisectors. With slopes and midpoints you can write each one.
points: Median from A: the line through A and the midpoint of BC.
Altitude from A: through A, perpendicular to BC (slope = −1/slope of BC).
Perpendicular bisector of PQ: through the midpoint of PQ, perpendicular to PQ.
Line parallel to Ax + By + C = 0 through (x₁, y₁): Ax + By = Ax₁ + By₁ (same A, B).
Line perpendicular to Ax + By + C = 0 through (x₁, y₁): Bx − Ay = Bx₁ − Ay₁ (swap A, B and change one sign).

example.q: Find the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining (1, 2) and (5, 6).
steps: Slope of segment: (6 − 2)/(5 − 1) = 1, so perpendicular slope −1.

learn.reallife: Surveyors locating a new well equidistant from two villages use the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining them.

games.title: Triangle line ↔ what it passes through
pairs: A and the midpoint of BC
Midpoint of BC, perpendicular to BC
Line parallel to BC through A

quiz.q: The line through (−2, 3) perpendicular to 3x − 4y + 2 = 0 is:
quiz.explain: Perpendicular: 4x + 3y + k = 0. Substitute: −8 + 9 + k = 0 ⇒ k = −1.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the same coefficients (parallel line)

quiz.q: Triangle A(2, 1), B(4, 3), C(6, 1). The median from B passes through:
quiz.explain: The midpoint of AC is ((2 + 6)/2, (1 + 1)/2) = (4, 1).
quiz.mistake: Takes the midpoint of AB or BC

quiz.q: In the same triangle, the median from B has equation:
quiz.explain: B(4, 3) and (4, 1) have the same x-coordinate, so the median is the vertical line x = 4.
quiz.mistake: Tries to compute a slope and divides by zero

quiz.q: Triangle A(0, 0), B(4, 0), C(1, 3). The altitude from A is perpendicular to BC. Its equation is:
quiz.explain: Slope BC = (3 − 0)/(1 − 4) = −1, so the altitude has slope 1 and passes through the origin: y = x.
quiz.mistake: Uses the slope of BC itself

quiz.q: The perpendicular bisector of the segment from (3, 4) to (−1, 2) is:
quiz.explain: Midpoint (1, 3); segment slope (2 − 4)/(−1 − 3) = 1/2, so perpendicular slope −2: y − 3 = −2(x − 1) ⇒ 2x + y − 5 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to use the midpoint

quiz.q: Which line is parallel to 2x + 5y − 7 = 0 and passes through the origin?
quiz.explain: Same A and B for parallel lines; through (0, 0) the constant is 0.
quiz.mistake: Swaps coefficients, giving a perpendicular line

quiz.q: The line through (1, 2) perpendicular to the line x − 2y + 3 = 0 has slope:
quiz.explain: Slope of x − 2y + 3 = 0 is 1/2; perpendicular slope −2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the reciprocal without the minus sign

quiz.q: For what value of p is the line px + 4y − 7 = 0 parallel to 3x + 2y + 1 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Equates p with 3 directly

teach.ask: Gappu must find the altitude of a triangle from vertex A. Explain how to write altitudes, medians and lines parallel or perpendicular to a given line.
teach.praise: Medians use midpoints, altitudes use perpendicular slopes, and parallels keep the same slope. Triangle tools ready!
teach.nudge: For an altitude, how is its slope related to the slope of the opposite side?

topics.title: Distance of a point from a line

learn.hook: How far is your house from a straight highway? Not along any road — the shortest distance, straight across at a right angle. One formula gives it.
points: The perpendicular distance of (x₁, y₁) from Ax + By + C = 0 is d = |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²).
It is derived by finding the area of the triangle formed by P and the intercepts of the line in two ways (½ × base × height and by coordinates).
Distance between parallel lines Ax + By + C₁ = 0 and Ax + By + C₂ = 0: |C₁ − C₂|/√(A² + B²).
Make sure both parallel lines have the SAME A and B before using the formula (e.g. rewrite 6x + 8y + 10 = 0 as 3x + 4y + 5 = 0).
Points at a given distance from a line: set the distance formula equal to the value and solve with ±.

example.q: Find the distance of (2, 3) from 3x + 4y − 3 = 0.

learn.reallife: Mobile tower engineers check the perpendicular distance from a planned tower to a straight railway line to meet safety rules.

quiz.q: Find the distance of (1, −2) from 4x − 3y + 5 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by √(A² + B²)

quiz.q: Find the distance between the parallel lines 3x − 4y + 7 = 0 and 3x − 4y − 8 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 8 from 7 without the sign

quiz.q: Find the distance between 6x + 8y − 5 = 0 and 3x + 4y + 5 = 0.
quiz.mistake: Uses the formula without making A and B equal

quiz.q: The distance of the origin from x/3 + y/4 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses the intercepts directly

quiz.q: Which points on the x-axis are at distance 2 from 3x + 4y − 6 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Keeps only the + case

quiz.q: The distance between the lines y = 2x + 3 and y = 2x − 2 is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets the √(A² + B²) step

quiz.q: If the distance of (k, 1) from 3x − 4y + 1 = 0 is 2, which is a possible value of k?
quiz.mistake: Drops the ± and solves 3k + 3 = 10

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The distance of (0, 0) from 5x + 12y − 13 = 0 is 1.
Reason (R): The distance of (x₁, y₁) from Ax + By + C = 0 is |Ax₁ + By₁ + C|/√(A² + B²).
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: |−13|/√(25 + 144) = 13/13 = 1, using exactly the formula in R.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the absolute value and gets −1

teach.ask: Gappu wants the shortest distance from his nest to a straight power line 3x + 4y − 12 = 0. Explain the distance formula and how to use it for parallel lines.
must: root of a squared plus b squared
teach.praise: Substitute, take the modulus, divide by √(A² + B²). Shortest flight path found!
teach.nudge: After substituting the point into the line, what do you divide by?

topics.title: Feet, images, concurrency and mixed problems

learn.hook: A ray of light bounces off a mirror at the same angle it hits. Coordinate geometry finds exactly where — using images of points in lines.
points: Foot of the perpendicular from P to a line: the point on the line where the perpendicular through P meets it.
Image (reflection) of P in a line: the line is the perpendicular bisector of P and its image P′. The midpoint of PP′ lies on the line and PP′ is perpendicular to it.
Lines with equal intercepts: x + y = a. Through a point (x₁, y₁): a = x₁ + y₁.
Three lines are concurrent if the intersection of two of them lies on the third.
Reflection problems: the image of the source in the mirror line, joined to the target point, gives the reflected ray.

example.q: Find the image of (2, 1) in the line x + y − 5 = 0.
steps: Let the image be (h, k). PP′ is perpendicular to the line (slope −1), so PP′ has slope 1: (k − 1)/(h − 2) = 1 ⇒ k = h − 1.
Midpoint ((h + 2)/2, (k + 1)/2) lies on the line: (h + 2)/2 + (k + 1)/2 = 5 ⇒ h + k = 7.

learn.reallife: Snooker and carrom players aim at a cushion's 'image point' to bank a shot — the same reflection geometry.

games.title: Find k so that x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 and kx + 3y = 8 are concurrent
Mixed line facts
items: The image of (3, 5) in the x-axis is (3, −5).
Reflection in y = 0 changes the sign of y.
The image of (1, 2) in the line y = x is (2, 1).
Reflection in y = x swaps the coordinates.
The foot of the perpendicular from (0, 0) to x + y = 2 is (2, 0).
It is (1, 1); (2, 0) is only the x-intercept.
The line through (2, 3) with equal intercepts is x + y = 5.
Three lines are concurrent if all three are parallel.
Parallel lines never meet; concurrent lines pass through one common point.

quiz.q: The foot of the perpendicular from (0, 0) to the line x + y = 4 is:
quiz.explain: The perpendicular from the origin is y = x; it meets x + y = 4 at (2, 2).
quiz.mistake: Picks an intercept point

quiz.q: The image of (4, 1) in the line x + y = 0 is:
quiz.explain: Reflection in y = −x sends (a, b) to (−b, −a), so (4, 1) → (−1, −4).
quiz.mistake: Uses the rule for y = x

quiz.q: Find k so that the lines x + y = 3, 2x − y = 0 and kx + 3y = 8 are concurrent.
quiz.explain: The first two meet at (1, 2). Then k(1) + 3(2) = 8 ⇒ k = 2.
quiz.mistake: Substitutes into the wrong line

quiz.q: The equation of the line through (4, −1) making equal intercepts on the axes is:
quiz.explain: x + y = a with a = 4 + (−1) = 3.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the coordinates

quiz.q: Find the foot of the perpendicular from (1, 3) to the line y = x.
quiz.explain: The perpendicular through (1, 3) has slope −1: y − 3 = −(x − 1), i.e. x + y = 4. It meets y = x at (2, 2).
quiz.mistake: Gives the image (3, 1) instead of the foot

quiz.q: If the foot of the perpendicular from P(1, 3) to a line is (2, 2), what is the image of P in that line?
quiz.explain: The foot is the midpoint of P and its image: image = 2(2, 2) − (1, 3) = (3, 1).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the foot with the image

quiz.q: A ray from (1, 2) is reflected by the x-axis and then passes through (5, 3). At which point does it meet the x-axis?
quiz.explain: Image of (1, 2) in the x-axis is (1, −2). The line through (1, −2) and (5, 3) has slope 5/4; it meets y = 0 at x = 1 + 2 × 4/5 = 13/5.
quiz.mistake: Joins (1, 2) directly to (5, 3)

quiz.q: Find the acute angle between the lines x − √3 y = 0 and √3 x − y = 0.
quiz.explain: Slopes 1/√3 and √3 (inclinations 30° and 60°), so the angle is 30°.
quiz.mistake: Adds the inclinations

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know where a light ray from a torch hits a mirror line before reaching his eye. Explain images of points and the foot of the perpendicular.
teach.praise: Reflect the source, join it to the target, and the mirror point appears. Light-bending maths!
teach.nudge: How are a point, its image and the foot of the perpendicular related?

learn.hook: Slice an ice-cream cone straight across: a circle. Tilt the knife: an ellipse. Tilt more: a parabola, then a hyperbola. Four curves, one cone.
points: Conic sections (conics) are the curves obtained when a plane cuts a double cone. They describe planetary orbits (ellipses), telescope and headlight reflectors (parabolas) and more.
Rotate a line (generator) about a fixed line (axis) that it meets at the vertex V, keeping the angle α between them fixed: this gives a double-napped cone with semi-vertical angle α.
Let the cutting plane make angle β with the axis (not through V): β = 90° gives a circle; α < β < 90° an ellipse; β = α a parabola; 0 ≤ β < α a hyperbola (cutting both nappes).
If the plane passes through the vertex: α < β ≤ 90° gives a point; β = α gives a straight line (a generator); 0 ≤ β < α gives a pair of intersecting lines. These are degenerate conics.
Planets move in ellipses with the Sun at one focus (Kepler); car headlights and satellite dishes are parabolic.

example.q: A double cone has semi-vertical angle 30°. A plane not through the vertex makes an angle of 50° with the axis. What curve is formed?
steps: α < β < 90°, so the section is an ellipse.

learn.reallife: ISRO's Mangalyaan travelled on an elliptical transfer orbit before Mars captured it — orbital mechanics is conic sections in action.

games.title: Which conic? (α = semi-vertical angle, β = angle of plane with axis, plane not through vertex)

quiz.q: A plane perpendicular to the axis of the cone (not through the vertex) cuts it in a:
quiz.explain: β = 90° gives a circle.
quiz.mistake: Confuses 'perpendicular to the axis' with 'parallel to a generator'

quiz.q: When the cutting plane is parallel to a generator (β = α, plane not through vertex), the section is a:
quiz.explain: β = α gives a parabola, which is open and has one branch.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the parabola and hyperbola conditions

quiz.q: Which section cuts BOTH nappes of the cone?
quiz.explain: When β < α the plane is steep enough to meet both nappes, giving a hyperbola with two branches.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the parabola has two branches

quiz.q: If the plane passes through the vertex and α < β ≤ 90°, the section is:
quiz.explain: The plane meets the cone only at the vertex — a degenerate conic.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the degenerate cases

quiz.q: The semi-vertical angle of a cone is the angle between:
options: the cutting plane and the axis
quiz.explain: α is fixed as the generator rotates about the axis.
quiz.mistake: Confuses α with β

quiz.q: Which real-life object uses a parabola's shape?
quiz.explain: A bulb at the focus of a parabolic reflector sends light out in a parallel beam.
quiz.mistake: Thinks planetary orbits are parabolic

quiz.q: For α = 45° and β = 60° (plane not through the vertex), the section is:
quiz.explain: 45° < 60° < 90°, so it is an ellipse.
quiz.mistake: Reverses the inequality between α and β

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): The path of the Earth around the Sun is an ellipse.
Reason (R): An ellipse is obtained when the cutting plane is perpendicular to the axis of the cone.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true (Kepler's first law). R is false: a plane perpendicular to the axis gives a circle; an ellipse needs α < β < 90°.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the conditions for circle and ellipse

teach.ask: Gappu has an ice-cream cone and a knife. Explain how slicing a double cone at different angles gives a circle, ellipse, parabola and hyperbola.
teach.praise: Straight across — circle; tilted — ellipse; parallel to the side — parabola; steep — hyperbola! Tasty maths.
teach.nudge: What happens when the plane is parallel to a generator?

learn.hook: A cricket ground's boundary rope is a circle around the pitch — every point at the same distance from the centre. Write that as an equation and you've got (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r².
points: A circle is the set of all points in a plane at a fixed distance r (radius) from a fixed point (centre).
Centre (h, k), radius r: (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². Centre at the origin: x² + y² = r².
General form x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0 has centre (−g, −f) and radius √(g² + f² − c), when g² + f² − c > 0.
Completing squares is the safe method: group x-terms and y-terms and add the right constants.
The coefficients of x² and y² must be equal (and there is no xy term); divide through if they are equal but not 1.

example.q: Find the centre and radius of x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0.

learn.reallife: A Chennai lighthouse's beam that reaches 20 km out covers the circle x² + y² = 400 (in km) on a map centred at the lighthouse.

games.title: Complete the square for x² + y² + 8x − 10y − 8 = 0

quiz.q: The equation of the circle with centre (−2, 3) and radius 4 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses (x − 2) and (y + 3), flipping the centre's signs

quiz.q: What is the radius of x² + y² − 4x − 8y − 5 = 0?
quiz.mistake: Forgets to add the completed-square constants

quiz.q: What is the centre of 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 12y − 6 = 0?
quiz.explain: Divide by 2: x² + y² − 4x + 6y − 3 = 0, so centre (−g, −f) = (2, −3).
quiz.mistake: Forgets to divide by 2 first

quiz.q: The radius of 2x² + 2y² − 8x + 12y − 6 = 0 is:
quiz.explain: After dividing by 2: r = √(4 + 9 + 3) = √16 = 4.
quiz.mistake: Uses c = −6 without dividing by 2

quiz.q: Which equation represents a circle?
quiz.explain: A circle needs equal x² and y² coefficients and no xy term. x² + y² + 2x = 0 is (x + 1)² + y² = 1.
quiz.mistake: Accepts unequal coefficients

quiz.q: The circle with centre at the origin and radius 6 is:
quiz.explain: x² + y² = r² = 36.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the radius

quiz.q: For what value of k is x² + y² − 6x + 8y + k = 0 a circle of radius 5?
quiz.mistake: Sets k = r²

quiz.q: The circle (x − 1)² + (y − 1)² = 1 touches:
quiz.explain: The centre (1, 1) is at distance 1 from both axes, equal to the radius.
quiz.mistake: Checks only one axis

teach.ask: Gappu found x² + y² − 6x + 4y − 12 = 0 in his book and can't spot the circle. Explain how to find the centre and radius.
teach.praise: Group, complete the squares, and read off (3, −2) and 5. The circle was hiding in plain sight!
teach.nudge: What constant must you add to x² − 6x to make a perfect square?

learn.hook: Three ATM machines on a map — is there a circle through all of them? Conditions like 'passes through these points' or 'centre on this line' pin down a circle.
points: Start with (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² or x² + y² + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0, and use each condition to write an equation.
Through two points with centre on a given line: the centre is equidistant from both points (and on the line). Solve for (h, k), then r.
Through three points: substitute each into the general form to get three linear equations in g, f, c.
Position of a point (x₁, y₁) relative to x² + y² = r²: inside if x₁² + y₁² < r², on if =, outside if >.
A circle through the origin has c = 0 in the general form.

example.q: Find the circle through (0, 0) and (4, 0) whose centre lies on the line y = x.
steps: Centre (h, h). Equal distances to (0, 0) and (4, 0): h² + h² = (h − 4)² + h² ⇒ h² = h² − 8h + 16 ⇒ h = 2.

learn.reallife: Earthquake epicentres are located by drawing circles around three seismograph stations and finding where they meet.

games.title: Inside, on or outside x² + y² = 25?
Circle through (0, 0), (6, 0), (0, 8)
items: Then (6, 0) gives 36 + 12g = 0, so g = −3, and (0, 8) gives 64 + 16f = 0, so f = −4

quiz.q: The circle through (0, 0), (a, 0) and (0, b) is:
quiz.explain: c = 0 from the origin; (a, 0) gives a² + 2ga = 0 ⇒ 2g = −a; similarly 2f = −b.
quiz.mistake: Gets the signs of g and f wrong

quiz.q: Is the point (2.5, −4) inside, on or outside the circle x² + y² = 25?
quiz.mistake: Compares the coordinates with 5 directly

quiz.q: A circle passes through (1, 0) and (0, 3), and its centre lies on the line x − y = 1. Its centre is:
quiz.explain: Equal distances: (h − 1)² + k² = h² + (k − 3)² ⇒ h − 3k = −4. With h − k = 1: k = 5/2, h = 7/2.
quiz.mistake: Solves the simultaneous equations with a sign slip

quiz.q: A circle of radius 5 has its centre on the y-axis and passes through (3, 2). Which can be its centre?
quiz.mistake: Takes the centre at (0, 5)

quiz.q: The circle x² + y² − 6x − 8y = 0 passes through which point?
options: (6, 0) and nothing else on the axes
quiz.explain: There is no constant term, so (0, 0) satisfies it. (3, 4) is the centre.
quiz.mistake: Confuses the centre with a point on the circle

quiz.q: How many circles pass through three given non-collinear points?
quiz.explain: Three non-collinear points fix g, f and c uniquely — this is the circumcircle.
quiz.mistake: Thinks three points allow many circles

quiz.q: The circle with centre (2, 2) passing through the origin has radius:
quiz.mistake: Takes r = 2

quiz.q: If (k, 1) lies on x² + y² = 10 and k > 0, then k is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to subtract 1

teach.ask: Gappu knows a circle passes through two points and its centre is on a line. Explain how to find the circle, and how to test if a point is inside it.
teach.praise: Equal distances to both points plus the line gives the centre. And x² + y² < r² means inside!
teach.nudge: What is special about the distances from the centre to the two given points?

learn.hook: Throw a ball, aim a TV dish, design a headlight — all parabolas. Every point on one is exactly as far from a point (focus) as from a line (directrix).
points: A parabola is the set of points equidistant from a fixed line (directrix) and a fixed point (focus) not on it.
Axis: the line through the focus perpendicular to the directrix. Vertex: where the parabola meets its axis. Latus rectum: the chord through the focus perpendicular to the axis.
y² = 4ax: focus (a, 0), directrix x = −a, axis the x-axis, opens right. y² = −4ax: focus (−a, 0), directrix x = a, opens left.
x² = 4ay: focus (0, a), directrix y = −a, opens up. x² = −4ay: focus (0, −a), directrix y = a, opens down. (a > 0 throughout.)
Length of the latus rectum = 4a.

example.q: Find the focus, axis, directrix and latus rectum length of y² = 20x.
example.answer: Focus (5, 0), axis y = 0, directrix x = −5, latus rectum 20

learn.reallife: The big radio telescope dishes (such as GMRT near Pune) are parabolic: incoming parallel signals all bounce to the receiver at the focus.

games.title: Read a from the equation and give the latus rectum length

quiz.q: The focus of x² = −20y is:
quiz.explain: x² = −4ay with 4a = 20 ⇒ a = 5; focus (0, −a) = (0, −5).
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign

quiz.q: The directrix of y² = 14x is:
quiz.explain: 4a = 14 ⇒ a = 7/2; directrix x = −a.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a instead of a

quiz.q: The length of the latus rectum of x² = 10y is:
quiz.explain: Latus rectum = 4a and here 4a = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gives a = 5/2 instead of 4a

quiz.q: Which parabola has its focus at (0, 3)?
quiz.explain: Focus (0, a) with a = 3 means x² = 4ay = 12y.
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a = 3

quiz.q: A point on y² = 4ax is at distance 7 from the directrix x = −3. Its distance from the focus is:
quiz.explain: For every point on a parabola, distance to focus = distance to directrix.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts a from the distance

quiz.q: The parabola y² = −8x opens:
quiz.explain: y² = −4ax (a = 2) has focus (−2, 0), so it opens towards negative x.
quiz.mistake: Thinks y² always opens to the right

quiz.q: Which statement about the parabola y² = 4ax (a > 0) is false?
quiz.explain: The axis of y² = 4ax is the x-axis (y = 0).
quiz.mistake: Confuses the axis with the directrix direction

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): Every point of a parabola is equidistant from its focus and directrix.
Reason (R): The vertex of y² = 4ax lies midway between the focus (a, 0) and the directrix x = −a.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true. R is a consequence of A applied to one point (the vertex), not the explanation of A, which is the definition itself.
quiz.mistake: Treats a special case as the reason for the definition

teach.ask: Gappu wants to know what makes a curve a parabola and how to read its focus and directrix from y² = 20x. Explain.
teach.praise: Same distance from a point and a line — that's a parabola. And y² = 20x means a = 5. Dish aimed!
teach.nudge: Every point on a parabola is equally far from which two things?

learn.hook: Engineers designing a headlight need to know exactly where the bulb goes. Give them the depth and width of the reflector and the parabola's focus tells them.
points: From an equation: match it to one of the four standard forms, find a, then read the focus, axis, directrix and latus rectum.
From focus and directrix (vertex at origin): the focus tells the form; e.g. focus (7, 0) and directrix x = −7 give y² = 28x.
From vertex (0, 0) and focus: focus (0, −5) gives x² = −20y.
Through a point with a given axis: substitute the point to find a; e.g. y² = 4ax through (3, 6) gives 36 = 12a, so a = 3.
Applications: headlight and dish reflectors (bulb or receiver at the focus), parabolic arches, and cables of suspension bridges under uniform load.

example.q: A dish reflector is 24 cm wide and 4 cm deep at its centre. How far from the vertex is the focus?
steps: Place the vertex at the origin with the axis along the y-axis: x² = 4ay.

learn.reallife: The main cables of a suspension bridge carrying a uniformly loaded deck hang very nearly in the shape of a parabola.

games.title: Equation of the parabola with vertex (0, 0), axis along x-axis, through (3, 6)

quiz.q: The parabola with focus (0, −6) and directrix y = 6 is:
quiz.explain: a = 6 and the focus is below the vertex, so x² = −4ay = −24y.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the side of the focus

quiz.q: The parabola with vertex (0, 0), axis along the y-axis, passing through (2, 3) is:
quiz.mistake: Substitutes into y² = 4ax instead

quiz.q: A parabolic dish is 16 cm wide and 4 cm deep at its centre. How far from the vertex is its focus?
quiz.explain: x² = 4ay through (8, 4): 64 = 16a ⇒ a = 4 cm.
quiz.mistake: Uses the full width 16 instead of half the width

quiz.q: The focus of x² = 9y lies at:
quiz.mistake: Takes a = 9

quiz.q: An equilateral triangle is inscribed in y² = 4ax with one vertex at the origin. Its side is 8a√3. For y² = 4x, the side is:
quiz.explain: Here a = 1, so the side is 8√3. (The other vertices are (12a, ±4√3 a).)
quiz.mistake: Uses 4a instead of a

quiz.q: The latus rectum of the parabola through (−3, 6) with vertex at the origin and axis along the x-axis has length:
quiz.explain: y² = 4ax through (−3, 6): 36 = −12a, so a = −3 and the parabola is y² = −12x. The latus rectum is 4|a| = 12.
quiz.mistake: Takes 4a as 6

quiz.q: Why is the bulb of a car headlight placed at the focus of the parabolic reflector?
options: Light from the focus reflects off the parabola into a beam parallel to the axis
The focus is the hottest point
Light from the focus spreads in all directions
The focus is the deepest point
quiz.explain: This reflective property of the parabola turns a point source into a parallel beam.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the focus is the vertex

quiz.q: Which parabola has its directrix x = 4 and vertex at the origin?
quiz.explain: Directrix x = a for y² = −4ax with a = 4, so y² = −16x.
quiz.mistake: Uses directrix x = −a

teach.ask: Gappu is building a solar cooker with a parabolic dish 24 cm wide and 4 cm deep. Explain how to find where to put the cooking pot (the focus).
teach.praise: Put the rim point into x² = 4ay, find a, and the pot goes a cm above the vertex. Dinner's cooking!
teach.nudge: Which point on the dish do you substitute into the equation?

topics.title: Ellipse: definition, parts and standard form

learn.hook: Tie a string to two pins, pull it tight with a pencil and draw: you get an ellipse. The sum of distances to the two pins never changes.
points: An ellipse is the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (foci) have a constant sum, 2a.
Centre: midpoint of the foci. Major axis (length 2a) passes through the foci; minor axis (length 2b) is perpendicular to it. c = distance from centre to a focus, and c² = a² − b².
Major axis along x-axis: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 (a > b), foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0). Along y-axis: x²/b² + y²/a² = 1, foci (0, ±c).
Derivation: from PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a with F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0), isolate one root, square twice and use b² = a² − c².
Eccentricity e = c/a, and 0 < e < 1. As e → 0 the ellipse becomes nearly a circle.

example.q: For x²/25 + y²/9 = 1, find a, b, c, the foci and the eccentricity.
steps: a² = 25, b² = 9 (larger denominator under x², so major axis on the x-axis).

learn.reallife: Earth's orbit is an ellipse with e ≈ 0.017 — so nearly circular that the Earth–Sun distance changes by only about 3% over a year.

games.title: Derive the ellipse equation
items: Take foci F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0) and PF₁ + PF₂ = 2a
Square and simplify: a − (c/a)x = √((x − c)² + y²)
Square again: x²(a² − c²)/a² + y² = a² − c²
Put b² = a² − c²: x²/a² + y²/b² = 1

quiz.q: For x²/16 + y²/25 = 1, the major axis lies along:
quiz.explain: 25 > 16 and 25 is under y², so a² = 25 lies along the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the major axis is always on the x-axis

quiz.q: The foci of x²/16 + y²/25 = 1 are:
quiz.explain: c² = 25 − 16 = 9, c = 3, along the major (y) axis.
quiz.mistake: Adds a² and b² as for a hyperbola

quiz.q: The eccentricity of x²/169 + y²/144 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses b/a

quiz.q: A point P is on an ellipse with foci F₁, F₂ and major axis length 10. What is PF₁ + PF₂?
quiz.explain: By definition the sum is constant and equals 2a = the major axis length.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the sum changes with P

quiz.q: Which value can the eccentricity of an ellipse take?
quiz.explain: For an ellipse 0 < e < 1.
quiz.mistake: Thinks e can be 1 or more

quiz.q: For an ellipse with a = 5 and c = 3, what is b?
quiz.mistake: Uses b² = a² + c²

quiz.q: The length of the minor axis of 16x² + 25y² = 400 is:
quiz.explain: x²/25 + y²/16 = 1: b = 4, minor axis 2b = 8.
quiz.mistake: Gives b instead of 2b

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): In an ellipse, a > c.
Reason (R): The sum of the distances of any point from the foci, 2a, is greater than the distance between the foci, 2c.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: For any point P not on the segment F₁F₂, PF₁ + PF₂ > F₁F₂ (triangle inequality), so 2a > 2c. R explains A.
quiz.mistake: Does not see why a must exceed c

teach.ask: Gappu drew a curve with two pins and a string. Explain why it's an ellipse and what a, b, c and e mean.
teach.praise: Two pins, a fixed sum, and c² = a² − b². And e < 1 always. Pin-tastic!
teach.nudge: What stays the same as the pencil moves around the two pins?

learn.hook: Ellipse questions in board exams are 'read off everything' or 'build from clues'. Master a, b, c and these become free marks.
points: Latus rectum: a chord through a focus perpendicular to the major axis; its length is 2b²/a.
From an equation: write it as x²/A + y²/B = 1. The larger denominator is a² and tells the direction of the major axis. Then c, foci, vertices, e and latus rectum follow.
From clues: vertices give a, foci give c, and b² = a² − c². Ends of the minor axis give b.
Through a point: substitute it into x²/a² + y²/b² = 1 to get a relation.
Rod sliding between the axes: if a point P on a rod AB (A on the x-axis, B on the y-axis) has PA = p and PB = q, P traces x²/q² + y²/p² = 1.

example.q: Find the equation of the ellipse with vertices (±10, 0) and foci (±6, 0).

learn.reallife: The arches of many old bridges and the 'whispering galleries' of some domes are elliptical: a whisper at one focus is heard clearly at the other.

games.title: Clues ↔ ellipse
pairs: Ends of major axis (±3, 0), minor axis (0, ±2)
Rod 10 cm, PA = 4 cm, PB = 6 cm

quiz.q: The length of the latus rectum of x²/36 + y²/16 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses 2a²/b

quiz.q: The ellipse with foci (0, ±5) and major axis 26 has equation:
quiz.explain: a = 13, c = 5, b² = 169 − 25 = 144. Major axis on the y-axis, so a² goes under y².
quiz.mistake: Puts a² under x² though the foci are on the y-axis

quiz.q: The eccentricity of 9x² + 25y² = 225 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses b/a = 3/5

quiz.q: An ellipse with centre at the origin and major axis on the x-axis passes through (2, 3) and (4, 1). What is a²?
quiz.mistake: Solves the linear system with a slip

quiz.q: A rod of length 15 cm moves with its ends on the axes. The point P on it with PA = 5 cm (A on the x-axis) traces:
quiz.explain: PB = 10 cm, and P traces x²/PB² + y²/PA² = 1, i.e. x²/100 + y²/25 = 1.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the two distances

quiz.q: The vertices of x²/49 + y²/36 = 1 are:
quiz.explain: a² = 49 under x², so vertices are (±a, 0) = (±7, 0).
quiz.mistake: Gives the foci or the minor-axis ends

quiz.q: An elliptical arch spans 8 m at its base and is 2 m high at the centre. How high is it 2 m from the centre?
quiz.mistake: Uses the full span 8 as a

quiz.q: For an ellipse, the distance between the foci is 8 and the minor axis is 6. What is the major axis length?
quiz.explain: c = 4, b = 3, a² = b² + c² = 25 ⇒ a = 5; major axis 2a = 10.
quiz.mistake: Gives a instead of 2a

teach.ask: Gappu's question gives vertices (±10, 0) and foci (±6, 0). Explain how to build the ellipse equation and find its latus rectum.
teach.praise: Vertices give a, foci give c, then b² = a² − c². And the latus rectum is 2b²/a. Equation built!
teach.nudge: Once you know a and c, how do you get b?

topics.title: Hyperbola: definition, parts and standard form

learn.hook: Hear a thunderclap at two places a known time apart and you know the difference of your distances from the lightning — so it lies on a hyperbola.
points: A hyperbola is the set of points whose distances from two fixed points (foci) have a constant difference, 2a (taken as positive).
Transverse axis: through the foci, length 2a between the vertices. Conjugate axis: perpendicular, length 2b. c = centre-to-focus distance, and c² = a² + b².
Transverse axis on x-axis: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1, foci (±c, 0), vertices (±a, 0). On y-axis: y²/a² − x²/b² = 1, foci (0, ±c).
Derivation: from |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a, square twice and use b² = c² − a².
Eccentricity e = c/a > 1 (since c > a). Unlike the ellipse, a need not be larger than b.

example.q: For x²/25 − y²/144 = 1, find the foci, vertices and eccentricity.
steps: a² = 25, b² = 144 (the positive term is under x², so the transverse axis is the x-axis).

learn.reallife: Hyperbolic paths appear in long-range radio navigation: a receiver measuring the time difference of signals from two stations lies on a hyperbola.

games.title: Derive the hyperbola equation
items: Foci F₁(−c, 0), F₂(c, 0) and PF₁ − PF₂ = 2a
Square and simplify: (c/a)x − a = √((x − c)² + y²)
Square again: x²(c² − a²)/a² − y² = c² − a²
Put b² = c² − a²: x²/a² − y²/b² = 1

quiz.q: For y²/36 − x²/64 = 1, the foci are:
quiz.explain: c² = 36 + 64 = 100, c = 10, on the y-axis (the positive term is y²).
quiz.mistake: Subtracts as for an ellipse

quiz.q: The eccentricity of x²/9 − y²/16 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses c² = a² − b²

quiz.q: Which value can the eccentricity of a hyperbola take?
quiz.explain: For a hyperbola e > 1.
quiz.mistake: Confuses with an ellipse

quiz.q: The length of the transverse axis of 16x² − 9y² = 144 is:
quiz.explain: x²/9 − y²/16 = 1: a = 3, transverse axis 2a = 6.
quiz.mistake: Gives the conjugate axis 2b = 8

quiz.q: For a point on a hyperbola with vertices (±4, 0), the difference of its distances from the foci is:
quiz.explain: |PF₁ − PF₂| = 2a = 8, the distance between the vertices.
quiz.mistake: Gives a instead of 2a

quiz.q: For a hyperbola, which relation is correct?
quiz.explain: For a hyperbola the foci lie beyond the vertices, and c² = a² + b².
quiz.mistake: Uses the ellipse relation

quiz.q: Which equation is a hyperbola with transverse axis along the y-axis?
quiz.explain: The positive term is under y², so the transverse axis is the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Looks at the larger denominator instead of the positive term

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): For x²/4 − y²/9 = 1, b > a is allowed.
Reason (R): In a hyperbola, a is always greater than b.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: Here a = 2, b = 3 and it is a valid hyperbola, so A is true. R is false: only c > a is required; b can be larger or smaller than a.
quiz.mistake: Carries over the ellipse rule a > b

teach.ask: Gappu confuses the ellipse and hyperbola formulas. Explain the hyperbola's definition, c² = a² + b², and why e > 1.
teach.praise: Ellipse adds distances, hyperbola subtracts them — and c² = a² + b² so e > 1. No more mix-ups!
teach.nudge: For a hyperbola, is it the sum or the difference of focal distances that stays constant?

topics.title: Hyperbola problems and mixed conic problems

learn.hook: Board papers love a 'find everything' hyperbola question and a twist problem mixing parabolas and real objects. Let's practise both.
points: Latus rectum of a hyperbola: length 2b²/a.
From an equation: bring it to x²/a² − y²/b² = 1 or y²/a² − x²/b² = 1; the positive term gives the transverse axis.
From clues: vertices give a, foci give c, b² = c² − a². A given transverse/conjugate axis gives 2a or 2b.
Through a point: substitute it to find the unknown.
Mixed problems: parabolic cables and dishes (use the vertex as origin and a rim or support point), and triangles inscribed in parabolas.

example.q: Find the hyperbola with foci (±10, 0) and transverse axis of length 12.

learn.reallife: The cooling towers of many thermal power stations have a hyperbolic profile — strong and material-saving.

quiz.q: The hyperbola with vertices (0, ±4) and foci (0, ±5) is:
quiz.explain: a = 4, c = 5, b² = 25 − 16 = 9; transverse axis on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Swaps a² and b²

quiz.q: The latus rectum length of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 is:
quiz.mistake: Uses 2a²/b

quiz.q: Find the hyperbola with foci (0, ±10) and conjugate axis of length 16.
quiz.explain: b = 8, c = 10, a² = 100 − 64 = 36; foci on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Uses c² for a²

quiz.q: Find a² if the hyperbola x²/a² − y²/4 = 1 passes through (3, 2).
quiz.mistake: Forgets the −y²/b² term

quiz.q: The vertices of 4y² − 9x² = 36 are:
quiz.explain: Divide by 36: y²/9 − x²/4 = 1, so a = 3 on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Reads a from the x² term

quiz.q: A parabolic suspension cable hangs between towers 100 m apart; it is 30 m above the road at the towers and 10 m at the centre. Taking the lowest point as (0, 0), the cable is x² = 4ay through (50, 20). What is 4a?
quiz.mistake: Uses the full height 30 m instead of 30 − 10 = 20 m

quiz.q: A satellite dish is 1 m wide and 0.125 m deep at the centre. Its receiver is placed at the focus. How far is it from the vertex?
quiz.mistake: Uses the full width as x

quiz.q: The foci of x²/16 − y²/9 = 1 and of the ellipse x²/25 + y²/9 = 1 compare as:
quiz.explain: Hyperbola: c² = 16 + 9 = 25. Ellipse: c² = 25 − 9 = 16.
quiz.mistake: Uses the same rule for both curves

teach.ask: Gappu gets 'foci (±10, 0), transverse axis 12' and must write the hyperbola. Explain the steps and how to find its latus rectum.
teach.praise: 2a from the transverse axis, c from the foci, b² = c² − a². Then 2b²/a. Hyperbola done!
teach.nudge: How is b² found for a hyperbola — c² + a² or c² − a²?

learn.hook: To tell an electrician exactly where a bulb hangs in a room, you need three numbers: how far along, how far across, and how high. Welcome to 3-D.
points: A point on a plane needs two coordinates; a point in space (a bulb hanging in a room) needs three.
Take three mutually perpendicular lines through a point O: the x-axis, y-axis and z-axis. O is the origin.
The axes determine three coordinate planes: the XY-plane (contains the x- and y-axes), the YZ-plane and the ZX-plane.
The three coordinate planes divide space into eight parts called octants.
Octants are named XOYZ, X′OYZ, X′OY′Z, XOY′Z, XOYZ′, X′OYZ′, X′OY′Z′, XOY′Z′ — numbered I to VIII.

example.q: How many octants, coordinate planes and coordinate axes are there in 3-D space?
steps: Three axes x, y, z through O.
Each pair of axes makes a coordinate plane: XY, YZ, ZX — three planes.
Three planes cut space into 8 octants.

learn.reallife: Air-traffic control at Delhi airport tracks each plane by two ground coordinates plus altitude — a point in 3-D space.

games.title: Match the 3-D vocabulary
pairs: Parts of space made by the three planes

games.title: Space basics
items: Three coordinate planes divide space into 8 octants.
Each plane splits space in two: 2 × 2 × 2 = 8.
The coordinate axes in 3-D are mutually perpendicular.
Each pair of axes meets at right angles at O.
The z-axis is perpendicular to the XY-plane, meeting it only at O.
A point in space needs exactly two coordinates.
It needs three: x, y and z.
The XY-plane and the YZ-plane meet along the y-axis.

quiz.q: How many octants are formed by the three coordinate planes?
quiz.explain: Each of the three planes divides space into two halves: 2³ = 8 octants.
quiz.mistake: Uses the 4 quadrants of the plane

quiz.q: The z-axis is perpendicular to which coordinate plane?
quiz.explain: The XY-plane contains the x- and y-axes, both perpendicular to the z-axis.
quiz.mistake: Picks a plane that contains the z-axis

quiz.q: The coordinate planes XY and ZX intersect along the:
quiz.explain: The x-axis is common to both the XY-plane and the ZX-plane.
quiz.mistake: Picks the axis missing from both names

quiz.q: Why does a point in space need three coordinates?
options: Because the plane has three axes
Because one coordinate is always zero
Space has three independent directions: length, breadth and height
quiz.explain: Two numbers fix a position on a floor; the third fixes the height above it.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the number of coordinates depends on the octants

quiz.q: How many coordinate planes are there in 3-D geometry?
quiz.explain: XY, YZ and ZX.
quiz.mistake: Counts the octants

quiz.q: Octant I (XOYZ) is bounded by:
options: the positive x-, y- and z-axes
quiz.explain: XOYZ uses OX, OY and OZ, the positive directions of all three axes.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the z-direction

quiz.q: Which line is common to all three coordinate planes?
options: None — they share only the origin
quiz.explain: Each pair of planes shares an axis, but no single line lies in all three; only O is common to all.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one axis lies in every plane

quiz.q: In a room, take one corner of the floor as the origin with two floor edges as the x- and y-axes. The vertical edge at that corner is the:
quiz.explain: The vertical edge is perpendicular to both floor edges, so it is the z-axis.
quiz.mistake: Treats the vertical edge as a plane

teach.ask: Gappu is used to graph paper with 2 axes. Explain how 3 axes, 3 coordinate planes and 8 octants describe space.
teach.praise: Three perpendicular axes, three planes, eight octants. Space is my new graph paper!
teach.nudge: How many parts do the three coordinate planes cut space into?

topics.title: Coordinates of a point in space

learn.hook: (2, −3, 5): go 2 along x, 3 backwards along y, 5 up. The signs tell you instantly which octant the point lives in.
points: The coordinates (x, y, z) of P are its (signed) perpendicular distances from the YZ-, ZX- and XY-planes respectively.
On the x-axis: (x, 0, 0); on the y-axis: (0, y, 0); on the z-axis: (0, 0, z). The origin is (0, 0, 0).
In the XY-plane: (x, y, 0); in the YZ-plane: (0, y, z); in the ZX-plane: (x, 0, z).
A point with any coordinate 0 lies on a coordinate plane (or axis), not inside an octant.

example.q: In which octants do (1, −2, 3) and (−4, 2, −5) lie?

learn.reallife: A warehouse robot in an e-commerce fulfilment centre locates a shelf bin by (aisle, rack, level) — three coordinates.

quiz.q: In which octant does (−3, 1, 2) lie?
quiz.explain: Signs (−, +, +) give octant II (X′OYZ).
quiz.mistake: Looks only at the x-sign

quiz.q: In which octant does (−4, −2, −5) lie?
quiz.explain: All three negative: octant VII.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up octants III and VII

quiz.q: A point lies on the x-axis. Which of its coordinates are zero?
quiz.explain: Every point on the x-axis has the form (x, 0, 0).
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coordinate named after the axis is zero

quiz.q: A point lies in the YZ-plane. Its coordinates have the form:
quiz.explain: The YZ-plane is x = 0.
quiz.mistake: Sets y and z to zero instead

quiz.q: The perpendicular distance of P(3, −4, 5) from the XY-plane is:
quiz.explain: Distance from the XY-plane is |z| = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the x-coordinate

quiz.q: The foot of the perpendicular from P(3, −4, 5) to the ZX-plane is:
quiz.explain: The ZX-plane is y = 0, so the foot keeps x and z and makes y = 0.
quiz.mistake: Makes the wrong coordinate zero

quiz.q: Which point lies in octant VIII?
quiz.explain: Octant VIII has signs (+, −, −).
quiz.mistake: Uses the order of signs for octant VI or V

quiz.q: Which point lies on a coordinate plane, not in any octant?
quiz.explain: y = 0 puts (5, 0, −2) on the ZX-plane.
quiz.mistake: Thinks negative coordinates mean 'outside every octant'

teach.ask: Gappu found the point (−2, 3, −4) and wants to know where it is. Explain what the three coordinates mean and how signs give the octant.
teach.praise: Each coordinate is a signed distance from a plane, and the three signs pick the octant. (−, +, −) is octant VI!
teach.nudge: What do the signs of x, y and z tell you about a point?

topics.title: Distance between two points in space

learn.hook: How long a cable do you need from a ceiling corner to the opposite floor corner? The 3-D distance formula is Pythagoras applied twice.
points: PQ = √((x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)² + (z₂ − z₁)²).
Derivation: draw a box with PQ as a diagonal; Pythagoras in the base gives PN² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)², then PQ² = PN² + (z₂ − z₁)².
Distance from the origin: OP = √(x² + y² + z²).
Collinearity: P, Q, R are collinear if one distance equals the sum of the other two (e.g. PQ + QR = PR).
Syllabus note: the section formula in 3-D is not part of the current rationalised syllabus for this chapter.

example.q: Show that A(1, 2, 3), B(2, 3, 4) and C(4, 5, 6) are collinear.
example.answer: Collinear, with B between A and C

learn.reallife: Architects in Mumbai's high-rises compute diagonal lengths of rooms for cables and ducts using √(l² + b² + h²).

games.title: Derive the 3-D distance formula
items: Draw a cuboid with PQ as a diagonal
In the base, PN² = (x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²
QN is vertical, so triangle PNQ is right-angled at N

quiz.q: Find the distance between (2, −1, 3) and (−2, 1, 3).
quiz.mistake: Adds the differences instead of squaring

quiz.q: The distance of (6, −2, 3) from the origin is:
quiz.mistake: Forgets to square the negative coordinate

quiz.q: A room is 4 m long, 3 m wide and 12 m high (a tall atrium). What is the length of the longest straight rod that fits?
quiz.explain: The space diagonal is √(16 + 9 + 144) = √169 = 13 m.
quiz.mistake: Uses only the floor diagonal

quiz.q: For P(1, 0, 2), Q(2, 1, 4) and R(4, 3, 8), PQ = √6 and QR = 2√6. What is PR, and are the points collinear?
quiz.explain: PR = √(9 + 9 + 36) = √54 = 3√6 = PQ + QR, so the points are collinear.
quiz.mistake: Compares only two of the three distances

quiz.q: If the distance between (k, 2, 1) and (1, 2, 1) is 3, which can k be?
quiz.mistake: Forgets the absolute value and takes k = 3

quiz.q: Which points are at distance 5 from the origin?
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates

quiz.q: The distance of P(3, 4, 5) from the z-axis is:
quiz.explain: The nearest point on the z-axis is (0, 0, 5); distance √(9 + 16) = 5.
quiz.mistake: Uses the z-coordinate as the distance

quiz.q:
Assertion (A): A(0, 0, 0), B(1, 1, 1) and C(2, 2, 2) are collinear.
Reason (R): AB + BC = AC.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
quiz.explain: AB = √3, BC = √3, AC = 2√3 = AB + BC. That equality is exactly the test for collinearity.
quiz.mistake: Does not connect the distance sum to collinearity

teach.ask: Gappu needs the length of a cable from one corner of his room's floor to the opposite ceiling corner. Explain the 3-D distance formula.
teach.praise: Square all three differences, add, take the root. Pythagoras goes 3-D!
teach.nudge: How many differences do you square in 3-D, and what do you do after adding them?

learn.hook: With just the distance formula you can prove a triangle is right-angled, find a missing corner of a parallelogram and even write the equation of a surface.
points: Triangle type: compute all three sides. Right-angled if the squares satisfy Pythagoras; isosceles if two sides are equal; equilateral if all three are equal.
Parallelogram ABCD: opposite sides equal (AB = CD, BC = DA). The missing vertex D = A + C − B (coordinate-wise), since the diagonals bisect each other.
Locus of P equidistant from A and B: PA² = PB²; the squared terms cancel, leaving a plane (the perpendicular bisector plane).
Locus of P with PA + PB = constant 2a (A, B the foci): an ellipsoid. With foci (±c, 0, 0): x²/a² + (y² + z²)/(a² − c²) = 1.
Points on an axis at a given distance: e.g. on the y-axis use (0, y, 0) and solve.

example.q: Find the equation of the set of points P equidistant from A(1, 0, 2) and B(3, 0, 0).
steps: Expand and cancel x², y², z²: −2x + 1 − 4z + 4 = −6x + 9.

learn.reallife: A drone delivery hub placed equidistant from two warehouses must lie on the perpendicular bisector plane of the line joining them.

games.title: Test ↔ conclusion
pairs: Sum of squares of two sides = square of third

items.text: Midpoint of B(0, 4, 0) and C(0, 0, 6) is ___
Triangle A(1, 0, 0), B(0, 1, 0), C(0, 0, 1) has every side ___
On the y-axis, points at distance 13 from (3, 4, 12) have y = 0 or ___

quiz.explain: AB = BC = CA = √2.
quiz.mistake: Assumes a 'corner' triangle is right-angled

quiz.q: Are A(0, 0, 0), B(3, 0, 0), C(3, 4, 0) the vertices of a right triangle?
quiz.explain: AB = 3, BC = 4, AC = 5 and 3² + 4² = 5², so the right angle is opposite AC, at B.
quiz.mistake: Places the right angle at the origin

quiz.q: The fourth vertex D of parallelogram ABCD with A(1, 2, 3), B(3, 4, 5), C(6, 5, 4) is:
quiz.mistake: Uses A + B − C instead

quiz.q: The locus of points equidistant from A(2, 0, 0) and B(0, 0, 2) is:
quiz.explain: (x − 2)² + y² + z² = x² + y² + (z − 2)² ⇒ −4x = −4z ⇒ x = z.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the squared terms

quiz.q: The length of the median from A(2, 0, 0) in triangle ABC with B(0, 4, 0), C(0, 0, 6) is:
quiz.explain: Midpoint of BC is (0, 2, 3). Distance from A = √(4 + 4 + 9) = √17.
quiz.mistake: Measures from A to B or C instead of the midpoint
